steps.title: 무슨 뜻이에요?
steps.title_en: What do you mean by that?
steps.goal: 애매한 말의 뜻을 묻고, 내 말을 풀어 설명하고, 상대 말을 정리해 확인하기
steps.scene_desc: 9월 첫 주 저녁, 그레이스네 거실. 지우가 노트북을 펼쳐 둔 채 머리를 긁적이며 이야기하고, 그레이스가 찻잔을 들고 웃으며 회의 진행자처럼 손짓함. 창가에 화분이 가득하고 창밖은 초가을 저녁 하늘(화면·벽에 글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "What do you mean by that?" (무슨 뜻이에요?). Goal: 애매한 말의 뜻을 묻고, 내 말을 풀어 설명하고, 상대 말을 정리해 확인하기. Today's scene: 9월 첫 주 저녁, 그레이스네 거실. 지우가 노트북을 펼쳐 둔 채 머리를 긁적이며 이야기하고, 그레이스가 찻잔을 들고 웃으며 회의 진행자처럼 손짓함. 창가에 화분이 가득하고 창밖은 초가을 저녁 하늘. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Grace, Jiwoo. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "What do you mean by ___?".

steps.when: 상대가 방금 쓴 말이나 생각을 설명해 달라고 할 때 써요.
steps.extra: What do you mean by “circle back”?
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "What do you mean by ___?" (~가 무슨 뜻이에요?). When to use it: 상대가 방금 쓴 말이나 생각을 설명해 달라고 할 때 써요. Note: What do you mean by “circle back”?
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "What I mean is ___.".

steps.when: 내가 한 말을 더 분명하게 다시 설명해요. *is* 뒤에는 완전한 문장.
steps.extra: What I mean is, let’s talk about it again later.
steps.teach:

steps.when: 상대의 말을 내 말로 정리해서 확인해요. 평서문 순서로 말하고 끝을 올려요.
steps.extra: So you’re saying we don’t need to decide today?

steps.title: New Team, New Words · 9월 첫 주 저녁, 그레이스네 거실에서

lines.en: So, how was your first video meeting with the Vancouver team?
lines.ko: 그래서, 밴쿠버 팀이랑 한 첫 화상 회의는 어땠어요?

lines.en: A bit confusing, to be honest. At the end, the team lead said, “Let’s circle back on this.” I just nodded.
lines.ko: 솔직히 좀 헷갈렸어요. 끝에 팀장님이 “Let’s circle back on this.”라고 했는데, 그냥 고개만 끄덕였어요.

lines.en: So, you mean you didn’t understand it, but you didn’t ask?
lines.ko: 그러니까 못 알아들었는데 물어보지 않았다는 거예요?

lines.en: Right. Then someone said, “That’s a quick win.” I was totally lost.
lines.ko: 네. 그다음엔 누가 “That’s a quick win.”이라고 했는데, 완전히 못 따라갔어요.

lines.en: Let’s practice. I’ll be the team lead. “Okay, everyone. Let’s circle back on this next week.”
lines.ko: 연습해 봐요. 제가 팀장 할게요. “자, 여러분. 이건 다음 주에 다시 이야기합시다.”

lines.en: Sorry, {{what do you mean by}} “circle back”?
lines.ko: 죄송한데, ‘circle back’이 무슨 뜻이에요?

lines.en: {{What I mean is}}, let’s talk about it again later.
lines.ko: 제 말은, 나중에 다시 이야기하자는 거예요.

lines.en: {{So you’re saying}} we don’t need to decide today?
lines.ko: 그러니까 오늘 결정하지 않아도 된다는 말씀이죠?

lines.en: Exactly. Now ask about the other one.
lines.ko: 바로 그거예요. 이제 다른 것도 물어봐요.

lines.en: And what do you mean by “a quick win”? Could you give me an example?
lines.ko: 그리고 ‘a quick win’은 무슨 뜻이에요? 예를 하나 들어 주시겠어요?

lines.en: Sure. It’s a small change that helps users right away, like a clearer button label.
lines.ko: 그럼요. 사용자에게 바로 도움이 되는 작은 변화예요. 버튼 이름을 더 알기 쉽게 바꾸는 것처럼요.

lines.en: Got it. In other words, it’s easy and useful. Next time, I’ll just ask!
lines.ko: 알겠어요. 다시 말해, 쉽고 쓸모 있는 거네요. 다음엔 그냥 물어볼게요!

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "New Team, New Words · 9월 첫 주 저녁, 그레이스네 거실에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Grace: "So, how was your first video meeting with the Vancouver team?" (그래서, 밴쿠버 팀이랑 한 첫 화상 회의는 어땠어요?)
2. Jiwoo: "A bit confusing, to be honest. At the end, the team lead said, “Let’s circle back on this.” I just nodded." (솔직히 좀 헷갈렸어요. 끝에 팀장님이 “Let’s circle back on this.”라고 했는데, 그냥 고개만 끄덕였어요.)
3. Grace: "So, you mean you didn’t understand it, but you didn’t ask?" (그러니까 못 알아들었는데 물어보지 않았다는 거예요?)
4. Jiwoo: "Right. Then someone said, “That’s a quick win.” I was totally lost." (네. 그다음엔 누가 “That’s a quick win.”이라고 했는데, 완전히 못 따라갔어요.)
5. Grace: "Let’s practice. I’ll be the team lead. “Okay, everyone. Let’s circle back on this next week.”" (연습해 봐요. 제가 팀장 할게요. “자, 여러분. 이건 다음 주에 다시 이야기합시다.”)
6. Jiwoo: "Sorry, what do you mean by “circle back”?" (죄송한데, ‘circle back’이 무슨 뜻이에요?)
7. Grace: "What I mean is, let’s talk about it again later." (제 말은, 나중에 다시 이야기하자는 거예요.)
8. Jiwoo: "So you’re saying we don’t need to decide today?" (그러니까 오늘 결정하지 않아도 된다는 말씀이죠?)
9. Grace: "Exactly. Now ask about the other one." (바로 그거예요. 이제 다른 것도 물어봐요.)
10. Jiwoo: "And what do you mean by “a quick win”? Could you give me an example?" (그리고 ‘a quick win’은 무슨 뜻이에요? 예를 하나 들어 주시겠어요?)
11. Grace: "Sure. It’s a small change that helps users right away, like a clearer button label." (그럼요. 사용자에게 바로 도움이 되는 작은 변화예요. 버튼 이름을 더 알기 쉽게 바꾸는 것처럼요.)
12. Jiwoo: "Got it. In other words, it’s easy and useful. Next time, I’ll just ask!" (알겠어요. 다시 말해, 쉽고 쓸모 있는 거네요. 다음엔 그냥 물어볼게요!)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. The learner plays Jiwoo in this lesson, so an answer in the first person (I'm new here instead of Jiwoo is new here) is right too; never correct that. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

First say in one short sentence that they will be Jiwoo and you will read Grace. Then go in order, one line at a time: call highlight_line with the line number before each line, read your line, and for the learner's line just wait for them to say it. If they say most of it or a good part of a long line, accept it warmly and go on; only if what they say is clearly not their line, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, give one short warm comment on how they did, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick true/false check about the scene.

Give the verdict in the language you are using with this learner. Only when you are speaking Korean to them, say it as 정답은 True예요 / 정답은 False예요. There are 3 statements: ask every one and wait for an answer to each (Oh or Hmm is not an answer). Only after you have checked the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

frame: What do you mean by ___? / Could you give me an example?
What I mean is ___. — So you’re saying ___?
head: 모르는 표현
다시 설명하기 (What I mean is …)
확인하기 (So you’re saying …?)
rows: let’s talk about it again later.
we don’t need to decide today?
it’s a small change that helps right away.
let’s look at it in detail.
we need more time for it?
we all understand it the same way.
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: What do you mean by ___? / Could you give me an example? / What I mean is ___. — So you’re saying ___? Table (모르는 표현 → 다시 설명하기 (What I mean is …)):
- “circle back” → let’s talk about it again later.
- “a quick win” → it’s a small change that helps right away.
- “a deep dive” → let’s look at it in detail.
- “on the same page” → we all understand it the same way.
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items: What I mean is … — 다시 설명하기

What do you mean by “circle back”? → *What I mean is*, let’s talk about it later. 
is 뒤에는 완전한 문장. 과거 That’s not *what I meant*. 그런 뜻이 아니었어요.

내 말로, 평서문 순서로, 끝을 올려요: *So you’re saying* we can wait? 그러니까 기다려도 된다는 거죠? 
대답: Exactly. 바로 그거예요. · Not quite. What I mean is … 꼭 그건 아니고요, 제 말은 …
errors: So you saying we can wait?
So you’re saying we can wait?
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- What I mean is … — 다시 설명하기: What do you mean by “circle back”? → What I mean is, let’s talk about it later. / is 뒤에는 완전한 문장. 과거 That’s not what I meant. 그런 뜻이 아니었어요.
- So you’re saying …? — 확인하기: 내 말로, 평서문 순서로, 끝을 올려요: So you’re saying we can wait? 그러니까 기다려도 된다는 거죠? / 대답: Exactly. 바로 그거예요. · Not quite. What I mean is … 꼭 그건 아니고요, 제 말은 …
Common mistakes on screen:
- What does mean “circle back”? → What does “circle back” mean? (묻는 표현은 does와 mean 사이에.)
- So you saying we can wait? → So you’re saying we can wait? (saying 앞에 are(you’re)가 있어야 해요.)
- Sorry, I misunderstanded. → Sorry, I misunderstood. (misunderstand는 불규칙 동사(understand → understood).)
There are 2 grammar points and 3 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: What I mean is … — 다시 설명하기: What do you mean by “circle back”? → What I mean is, let’s talk about it later. is 뒤에는 완전한 문장. 과거 That’s not what I meant. 그런 뜻이 아니었어요.
So you’re saying …? — 확인하기: 내 말로, 평서문 순서로, 끝을 올려요: So you’re saying we can wait? 그러니까 기다려도 된다는 거죠? 대답: Exactly. 바로 그거예요. · Not quite. What I mean is … 꼭 그건 아니고요, 제 말은 …
mistakes: What does mean “circle back”? → What does “circle back” mean?
So you saying we can wait? → So you’re saying we can wait?
Sorry, I misunderstanded. → Sorry, I misunderstood.

steps.note: 예) take it offline / talk about it after the meeting → A: What do you mean by “take it offline”? B: What I mean is, let’s talk about it after the meeting. A: So you’re saying …?
items: talk about it after the meeting
a number that’s close, not exact
time and energy for more work
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) take it offline / talk about it after the meeting → A: What do you mean by “take it offline”? B: What I mean is, let’s talk about it after the meeting. A: So you’re saying …? The items (the words the learner gets for each one): take it offline / talk about it after the meeting | a ballpark number / a number that’s close, not exact | bandwidth / time and energy for more work | touch base / have a short chat.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "What do you mean by that?" (무슨 뜻이에요?); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "What do you mean by ___?" / "What I mean is ___." / "So you’re saying ___?". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: Could you give me an example?
Let me put it another way.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 더 자세히 묻기: "Could you be more specific?" (좀 더 구체적으로 말씀해 주시겠어요?, 정중); "Could you give me an example?" (예를 하나 들어 주시겠어요?, 보통); "Just to be clear, ___." (확실히 해 두자면, ~., 정중); "Am I right in thinking ___?" (~라고 이해하면 맞을까요?, 정중)
- 다르게 말하기: "In other words, ___." (다시 말해, ~., 보통); "Let me put it another way." (다르게 말해 볼게요., 보통); "That’s not what I meant." (그런 뜻이 아니었어요., 보통)
- 확인하고 따라가기: "Does that make sense?" (이해되세요?, 보통); "I’m with you." (무슨 말인지 알겠어요. 계속하세요., 친근)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 뜻에 관한 낱말

*specify* 구체적으로 밝히다 · *precisely* 정확히 
a *distinction* 구별, 차이 · *distinguish* A from B A와 B를 구별하다 
*perceive* (어떻게) 받아들이다, 인식하다 · *perception* 인식, 보는 방식 
It’s true *in the sense that* … …라는 점에서는 맞아요
회사에서 쓰는 표현 (참고)

*circle back* (나중에) 다시 이야기하다 
a *quick win* 금방 얻을 수 있는 작은 성과 
a *deep dive* 깊이 자세히 살펴보기 
이 책의 밴쿠버 팀과 자전거 공유 앱은 수업용으로 지어낸 이야기예요.
steps.blank:
A: What do you mean ___ “circle back”?   B: What I mean ___, let’s talk about it later. 
A: So you’re ___ we don’t need to decide today?   B: Exactly. Does that make ___? 
낱말 상자: by · is · saying · sense
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 뜻에 관한 낱말: specify 구체적으로 밝히다 · precisely 정확히 / a distinction 구별, 차이 · distinguish A from B A와 B를 구별하다 / perceive (어떻게) 받아들이다, 인식하다 · perception 인식, 보는 방식 / It’s true in the sense that … …라는 점에서는 맞아요
- 회사에서 쓰는 표현 (참고): circle back (나중에) 다시 이야기하다 / a quick win 금방 얻을 수 있는 작은 성과 / a deep dive 깊이 자세히 살펴보기 / 이 책의 밴쿠버 팀과 자전거 공유 앱은 수업용으로 지어낸 이야기예요.
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: What do you mean ___ “circle back”? B: What I mean ___, let’s talk about it later. / A: So you’re ___ we don’t need to decide today? B: Exactly. Does that make ___? / 낱말 상자: by · is · saying · sense
Go through every point in each tip box (for example every greeting with its time of day), one or two short sentences each, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, one blank per turn: stop at the blank, wait for them to fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: clear (분명한, 알기 쉬운), clarify (분명하게 설명하다), example (예, 보기), misunderstand (잘못 알아듣다, 오해하다), summary (요약), rephrase (다른 말로 바꿔 말하다), statement ((공식적인) 발언, 진술), communicate (소통하다, 생각을 전하다), distinguish (구별하다), explanation (설명), interpret ((뜻을) 해석하다, 받아들이다), confusion (혼란, 헷갈림).
Go through about six, new ones first, one word per turn: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and wait for the learner to say it before the next word. Never give several words in one turn. After every two or three words, ask one tiny real question with the word you just did (for example: Are you a morning person?), wait for the answer and react; do this at least twice in this part. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

Word list on screen: specific (구체적인, 자세한) — "Be more specific."; sense (뜻, 의미(make sense 이해가 되다)) — "Does that make sense?"; interpretation (해석, 이해한 방식) — "my interpretation"; mean (~라는 뜻이다, ~라는 뜻으로 말하다) — "What do you mean?"; meaning (뜻, 의미) — "the meaning of “circle back”"; explain (설명하다) — "Could you explain it again?"; confuse (헷갈리게 하다) — "Fast speech confuses me."; point (요점, 하려는 말) — "I see your point."; detail (세부 사항(in detail 자세히)) — "in detail"; exactly (정확히; (대답) 바로 그거예요) — "Exactly!"; check (확인하다) — "Let me check I understand.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: Have you ever misunderstood someone in English? What happened?
Yes. I thought ___ meant ___. / Not that I remember.
A coworker says, “Let’s take it offline.” You don’t know it. What do you say?
Sorry, what do you mean by “take it offline”?
Explain a Korean word or phrase in English.
It’s ___. What I mean is ___. In other words, ___.
I say, “I’m not a morning person.” Check what I mean.
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Have you ever misunderstood someone in English? What happened?" (hint on screen: Yes. I thought ___ meant ___. / Not that I remember.)
- "A coworker says, “Let’s take it offline.” You don’t know it. What do you say?" (hint on screen: Sorry, what do you mean by “take it offline”?)
- "Explain a Korean word or phrase in English." (hint on screen: It’s ___. What I mean is ___. In other words, ___.)
- "I say, “I’m not a morning person.” Check what I mean." (hint on screen: So you’re saying you ___?)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.
questions: Have you ever misunderstood someone in English? What happened?
A coworker says, “Let’s take it offline.” You don’t know it. What do you say?
Explain a Korean word or phrase in English.
I say, “I’m not a morning person.” Check what I mean.

steps.title: Yet Another Meeting
steps.text: The next Tuesday, at 9 a.m. in Seoul (5 p.m. the day before in Vancouver), Jiwoo joined *yet another* video meeting. The project is *run by* Maya and a lead in Vancouver, and the new version of the bike-sharing app is *set to* start user tests in November. The lead shared *the following* goal: “We *aim to* make returning a bike faster.” *Faced with* a new phrase, “a deep dive,” Jiwoo didn’t just nod this time. “Sorry, what do you mean by that? Could you specify?” The lead explained *in detail*. “It’s a deep dive *in the sense that* we’ll study every step of a return.” Later, Maya said, “Good question. Asking helps everyone get the exact meaning.” Asking wasn’t a weakness. It was clear communication.
steps.gloss: yet another 또 하나의 · run by ~가 이끄는 · set to ~할 예정인 · the following 다음의 · aim to ~하는 것을 목표로 하다 · faced with ~에 맞닥뜨려 · in detail 자세히 · in the sense that ~라는 점에서
questions: When is the app set to start user tests?
What did Jiwoo do when she heard “a deep dive”?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "Yet Another Meeting". Text: "The next Tuesday, at 9 a.m. in Seoul (5 p.m. the day before in Vancouver), Jiwoo joined yet another video meeting. The project is run by Maya and a lead in Vancouver, and the new version of the bike-sharing app is set to start user tests in November. The lead shared the following goal: “We aim to make returning a bike faster.” Faced with a new phrase, “a deep dive,” Jiwoo didn’t just nod this time. “Sorry, what do you mean by that? Could you specify?” The lead explained in detail. “It’s a deep dive in the sense that we’ll study every step of a return.” Later, Maya said, “Good question. Asking helps everyone get the exact meaning.” Asking wasn’t a weakness. It was clear communication." Words: yet another 또 하나의 · run by ~가 이끄는 · set to ~할 예정인 · the following 다음의 · aim to ~하는 것을 목표로 하다 · faced with ~에 맞닥뜨려 · in detail 자세히 · in the sense that ~라는 점에서.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "When is the app set to start user tests?" / "What did Jiwoo do when she heard “a deep dive”?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘What do you mean by ___?’로 상대가 한 말의 뜻을 물을 수 있어요.
‘What I mean is ___.’로 내 말을 더 분명하게 다시 설명할 수 있어요.
‘So you’re saying ___?’로 내가 제대로 이해했는지 확인할 수 있어요.
steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘What do you mean by ___?’로 상대가 한 말의 뜻을 물을 수 있어요.
- ‘What I mean is ___.’로 내 말을 더 분명하게 다시 설명할 수 있어요.
- ‘So you’re saying ___?’로 내가 제대로 이해했는지 확인할 수 있어요.
First ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence, and stop there to wait. React and praise specifically. Only then, in a later turn, end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to it, say that the next lesson is waiting for next time, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

lessons.title: 끼어들기
lessons.goal: 공손하게 끼어들고 말을 덧붙이고 넘겨주기

steps.title: 끼어들기
steps.goal: 공손하게 끼어들고 말을 덧붙이고 넘겨주기
steps.scene_desc: 9월 중순 토요일 오후, 동네 카페 앞 나무 벤치. 지우가 테이크아웃 커피를 든 채 지친 얼굴로 이야기하고, 옆에 앉은 벤이 회의하는 사람처럼 손을 들어 보이며 웃음. 길가 가로수에 초가을 햇살(간판·컵에 글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "Sorry to interrupt, but…" (끼어들기). Goal: 공손하게 끼어들고 말을 덧붙이고 넘겨주기. Today's scene: 9월 중순 토요일 오후, 동네 카페 앞 나무 벤치. 지우가 테이크아웃 커피를 든 채 지친 얼굴로 이야기하고, 옆에 앉은 벤이 회의하는 사람처럼 손을 들어 보이며 웃음. 길가 가로수에 초가을 햇살. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Ben, Jiwoo. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "Sorry to interrupt, but ___.".

steps.when: 남이 말하는 중에 정중하게 끼어들 때 써요.
steps.extra: Sorry to interrupt, but could I ask a quick question?
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "Sorry to interrupt, but ___." (말씀 중에 죄송한데, ~.). When to use it: 남이 말하는 중에 정중하게 끼어들 때 써요. Note: Sorry to interrupt, but could I ask a quick question?
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "Can I just add something?".

steps.when: 내 생각을 보탤 때 써요. *just*를 넣으면 더 부드럽고 공손해요.
steps.extra: Can I just add something? Users often ride at night.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "Can I just add something?" (하나만 덧붙여도 될까요?). When to use it: 내 생각을 보탤 때 써요. just를 넣으면 더 부드럽고 공손해요. Note: Can I just add something? Users often ride at night.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) Give a different everyday moment where they need it, and let them say it there.

steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: Sorry to interrupt, but ___. / Go ahead. / Sorry, go on. Table (끼어드는 말 → 하고 싶은 말):
- Sorry to interrupt, but… → could I ask a quick question?
- Can I just add something? → Users often ride at night.
- If I could just jump in here, … → the button is too small.
- Before we move on, … → can we check the timeline?
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
*Sorry to* interrupt, but … → Sorry to + 동사원형 
Sorry to bother you. 귀찮게 해서 죄송해요. 
이렇게도 써요: Sorry *for* interrupting. → Sorry for + -ing
just · Go ahead · Sorry, go on

Can I *just* add something? just(조금만) → 더 부드럽고 공손해요. 
Go ahead. 말씀하세요. 
Sorry, go on. 계속하세요(둘이 동시에 말을 꺼냈을 때).
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- Sorry to + 동사원형 — 정중하게 끼어들기: Sorry to interrupt, but … → Sorry to + 동사원형 / Sorry to bother you. 귀찮게 해서 죄송해요. / 이렇게도 써요: Sorry for interrupting. → Sorry for + -ing
- just · Go ahead · Sorry, go on: Can I just add something? just(조금만) → 더 부드럽고 공손해요. / Go ahead. 말씀하세요. / Sorry, go on. 계속하세요(둘이 동시에 말을 꺼냈을 때).
Common mistakes on screen:
- Sorry to interrupting, but… → Sorry to interrupt, but… (to 뒤에는 동사원형.)
- Can I just adding something? → Can I just add something? (can 뒤에는 동사원형.)
- Sorry for interrupt. → Sorry for interrupting. (for 뒤에는 -ing.)
- Where I was? → Where was I? (묻는 문장이라 was가 I 앞에.)
There are 2 grammar points and 4 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

steps.note: 예) ask a question / Is the test online? → Sorry to interrupt, but could I ask a quick question? Is the test online? — Sure, go ahead.
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) ask a question / Is the test online? → Sorry to interrupt, but could I ask a quick question? Is the test online? — Sure, go ahead. The items (the words the learner gets for each one): ask a question / Is the test online? | add something / Users ride at night. | a quick comment / The button is too small. | before we move on / Let’s check the timeline.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "Sorry to interrupt, but…" (끼어들기); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "Sorry to interrupt, but ___." / "Can I just add something?" / "Go ahead.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 끼어들기: "If I could just jump in here, ___." (여기서 잠깐 한 말씀 드리자면, ~., 정중); "Just a quick comment." (짧게 한마디만 할게요., 보통); "Before we move on, ___." (다음으로 넘어가기 전에, ~., 정중)
- 누가 끼어들 때: "Can I finish my point?" (제 얘기 마저 해도 될까요?, 보통); "Hold that thought." (잠깐만요, 그 얘기는 이따 해요., 친근); "Sorry, go on." (죄송해요, 계속하세요., 보통)
- 하던 이야기로 돌아가기: "Where was I?" (제가 어디까지 얘기했죠?, 친근); "As I was saying, ___." (아까 하던 말을 이어서 하면, ~., 보통); "I’d like to come back to ___." (~ 이야기로 다시 돌아가고 싶어요., 정중)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 회의에서 쓰는 말

*have the floor* 발언권이 있다 · speak *in turn* 차례대로 말하다 
*raise* a point 문제를 꺼내다 · a *string* of questions 줄줄이 이어진 질문 
The meeting *dragged on*. 회의가 질질 늘어졌어요. · *silence* 침묵
부드럽고 분명하게 (참고)

*No offense*, but … 기분 나쁘게 듣지는 마세요, 그런데 …(조심해서 써요) 
a *slight* change 약간의 변화 · First, … *Secondly*, … 첫째, … 둘째, … 
*Aside* from that, … 그것 말고는, …
steps.blank:
A: Sorry to ___, but can I just ___ something?   B: Sure, go ___. 
A: Oh, sorry. I cut you off.   B: No problem. Where ___ I? Oh, yes. As I was ___, … 
낱말 상자: interrupt · add · ahead · was · saying
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 회의에서 쓰는 말: have the floor 발언권이 있다 · speak in turn 차례대로 말하다 / raise a point 문제를 꺼내다 · a string of questions 줄줄이 이어진 질문 / The meeting dragged on. 회의가 질질 늘어졌어요. · silence 침묵
- 부드럽고 분명하게 (참고): No offense, but … 기분 나쁘게 듣지는 마세요, 그런데 …(조심해서 써요) / a slight change 약간의 변화 · First, … Secondly, … 첫째, … 둘째, … / Aside from that, … 그것 말고는, …
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: Sorry to ___, but can I just ___ something? B: Sure, go ___. / A: Oh, sorry. I cut you off. B: No problem. Where ___ I? Oh, yes. As I was ___, … / 낱말 상자: interrupt · add · ahead · was · saying
Go through every point in each tip box (for example every greeting with its time of day), one or two short sentences each, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, one blank per turn: stop at the blank, wait for them to fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: interrupt ((말을) 끊다, 끼어들다), comment ((짧은) 의견, 한마디), jump in ((대화에) 끼어들다), raise (들어 올리다; (문제를) 꺼내다), note (메모, 쪽지), quick (빠른; 짧은), remark ((짧은) 말, 발언), have the floor (발언권을 갖다), continue (계속하다), silence (침묵, 고요), turn (차례, 순서), add (더하다; 덧붙여 말하다).
Go through about six, new ones first, one word per turn: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and wait for the learner to say it before the next word. Never give several words in one turn. After every two or three words, ask one tiny real question with the word you just did (for example: Are you a morning person?), wait for the answer and react; do this at least twice in this part. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

Word list on screen: briefly (짧게, 간단히) — "Let me explain briefly."; finish (끝내다, 마치다) — "Can I finish my point?"; point (요점, 하려는 말) — "That’s a good point."; return ((하던 이야기로) 돌아가다) — "Let’s return to the map."; thought (생각) — "Hold that thought."; mention ((짧게) 언급하다, 말하다) — "You mentioned the map."; aside (옆으로, 따로(aside from ~ 말고는)) — "Aside from that, it’s fine."; slight (약간의, 조금의) — "a slight change"; secondly (둘째로) — "Secondly, the button is small.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: In meetings or classes, is it easy for you to interrupt?
Not really. I usually wait for a ___. / Yes, if it’s important.
Someone is talking, and you have a quick question. What do you say?
Someone jumps in, but you want to finish. What do you say?
Can I finish my point? / Hold that thought.
I’ll talk about my weekend. Jump in with a question.
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "In meetings or classes, is it easy for you to interrupt?" (hint on screen: Not really. I usually wait for a ___. / Yes, if it’s important.)
- "Someone is talking, and you have a quick question. What do you say?" (hint on screen: Sorry to interrupt, but ___?)
- "Someone jumps in, but you want to finish. What do you say?" (hint on screen: Can I finish my point? / Hold that thought.)
- "I’ll talk about my weekend. Jump in with a question." (hint on screen: Sorry to interrupt, but ___? (선생님 → “Go ahead.”))
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.
questions: In meetings or classes, is it easy for you to interrupt?
Someone is talking, and you have a quick question. What do you say?

I’ll talk about my weekend. Jump in with a question.

steps.title: The Next Meeting
steps.text: At the next weekly meeting, the Vancouver team shared *a range of* ideas for the new map. Jiwoo didn’t *hold back*. When there was a short silence, she said, “Sorry to interrupt, but can I just add something?” The lead said, “Go ahead. You have the floor.” Jiwoo spoke briefly *so as to* keep the meeting short. “First, many riders in Seoul ride at night. Secondly, the map icons are hard to see.” *By way of* example, she showed a slight change to one icon. Then came a string of questions, and she answered them *in turn*. Maya said, “Your idea will be *reflected in* the next version.” *In return for* Jiwoo’s help, a Vancouver designer shared his notes, and the lead *moved* her topic *up* to the top of next week’s list.
steps.gloss: a range of 여러 가지의 · hold back (할 말을) 참다 · so as to ~하기 위해 · by way of ~로서 · in turn 차례로 · reflected in ~에 반영된 · in return for ~에 대한 보답으로 · move up (순서를) 앞으로 올리다
questions: What did Jiwoo say when there was a short silence?
What did she show by way of example?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "The Next Meeting". Text: "At the next weekly meeting, the Vancouver team shared a range of ideas for the new map. Jiwoo didn’t hold back. When there was a short silence, she said, “Sorry to interrupt, but can I just add something?” The lead said, “Go ahead. You have the floor.” Jiwoo spoke briefly so as to keep the meeting short. “First, many riders in Seoul ride at night. Secondly, the map icons are hard to see.” By way of example, she showed a slight change to one icon. Then came a string of questions, and she answered them in turn. Maya said, “Your idea will be reflected in the next version.” In return for Jiwoo’s help, a Vancouver designer shared his notes, and the lead moved her topic up to the top of next week’s list." Words: a range of 여러 가지의 · hold back (할 말을) 참다 · so as to ~하기 위해 · by way of ~로서 · in turn 차례로 · reflected in ~에 반영된 · in return for ~에 대한 보답으로 · move up (순서를) 앞으로 올리다.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "What did Jiwoo say when there was a short silence?" / "What did she show by way of example?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘Sorry to interrupt, but ___.’로 정중하게 끼어들 수 있어요.
‘Can I just add something?’으로 내 생각을 덧붙일 수 있어요.
‘Go ahead.’와 ‘Sorry, go on.’으로 상대에게 말할 차례를 줄 수 있어요.
steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘Sorry to interrupt, but ___.’로 정중하게 끼어들 수 있어요.
- ‘Can I just add something?’으로 내 생각을 덧붙일 수 있어요.
- ‘Go ahead.’와 ‘Sorry, go on.’으로 상대에게 말할 차례를 줄 수 있어요.
First ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence, and stop there to wait. React and praise specifically. Only then, in a later turn, end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to it, say that the next lesson is waiting for next time, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

lessons.title: 일정 미루기
lessons.goal: 일정을 미루자고 하고 사정을 설명하고 계속 알리기

steps.title: 일정 미루기
steps.goal: 일정을 미루자고 하고 사정을 설명하고 계속 알리기
steps.scene_desc: 9월 말 목요일 오후, 지우 회사 창가 자리. 지우가 노트북 앞에서 휴대폰을 귀에 대고 미안한 표정으로 통화하고, 화면 한쪽 동그란 창(통화 화면 느낌)에 클로이가 자기 작업실에서 웃으며 손을 흔듦. 책상 위 탁상 달력과 메모지(화면·달력에 글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "Could we push it back?" (일정 미루기). Goal: 일정을 미루자고 하고 사정을 설명하고 계속 알리기. Today's scene: 9월 말 목요일 오후, 지우 회사 창가 자리. 지우가 노트북 앞에서 휴대폰을 귀에 대고 미안한 표정으로 통화하고, 화면 한쪽 동그란 창(통화 화면 느낌)에 클로이가 자기 작업실에서 웃으며 손을 흔듦. 책상 위 탁상 달력과 메모지. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Chloe, Jiwoo. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "Could we push it back to ___?".

steps.en: Could we push it back to ___?
steps.when: 약속이나 일정을 더 늦은 때로 옮기자고 정중하게 부탁해요.
steps.extra: Could we push it back to next Tuesday?
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "Could we push it back to ___?" (~로 미룰 수 있을까요?). When to use it: 약속이나 일정을 더 늦은 때로 옮기자고 정중하게 부탁해요. Note: Could we push it back to next Tuesday?
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "Something came up.".

steps.when: 일정을 바꾸는 이유를 짧게 말해요. 자세히 설명하지 않아도 돼요.
steps.extra: Sorry, something came up at work.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "Something came up." (일이 좀 생겼어요.). When to use it: 일정을 바꾸는 이유를 짧게 말해요. 자세히 설명하지 않아도 돼요. Note: Sorry, something came up at work.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) Give a different everyday moment where they need it, and let them say it there.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "I’ll keep you posted.".

steps.when: 새로운 소식을 나중에 전하겠다고 약속해요.
steps.extra: The date may change. I’ll keep you posted.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "I’ll keep you posted." (소식 있으면 알려 드릴게요.). When to use it: 새로운 소식을 나중에 전하겠다고 약속해요. Note: The date may change. I’ll keep you posted.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) Give a different everyday moment where they need it, and let them say it there.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("A Change of Plans · 9월 말 목요일, 전화 통화") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: A Change of Plans · 9월 말 목요일, 전화 통화

lines.en: Hi, Jiwoo! Are we still on for lunch tomorrow? I found a great new noodle place.
lines.ko: 지우 씨, 안녕하세요! 내일 점심 약속 그대로죠? 새로 생긴 좋은 국숫집을 찾았어요.

lines.en: Hi, Chloe. I’m so sorry, but {{something came up}}. We have an urgent design review tomorrow.
lines.ko: 안녕하세요, 클로이 씨. 정말 미안한데, 일이 좀 생겼어요. 내일 급한 디자인 검토 회의가 있어요.

lines.en: Oh no. On a Friday?
lines.ko: 저런. 금요일에요?

lines.en: Yes. The Vancouver team needs our new screens soon, and we’re a bit behind schedule.
lines.ko: 네. 밴쿠버 팀이 새 화면을 곧 받아야 하는데, 저희가 일정보다 좀 늦어졌어요.

lines.en: That sounds stressful. Don’t worry about lunch.
lines.ko: 스트레스받겠네요. 점심은 걱정하지 마요.

lines.en: Thanks. {{Could we push it back to}} next week? Maybe Monday?
lines.ko: 고마워요. 다음 주로 미룰 수 있을까요? 월요일 어때요?

lines.en: Hmm, Monday clashes with a video shoot. Would Tuesday suit you better?
lines.ko: 음, 월요일은 영상 촬영이랑 겹쳐요. 화요일이 더 괜찮아요?

lines.en: Tuesday works for me. Same time, twelve thirty?
lines.ko: 화요일 좋아요. 같은 시간, 12시 반이요?

lines.en: Perfect. Ooh, by the way, “Something came up.” You sounded like a busy boss in a TV drama!
lines.ko: 좋아요. 아, 그런데 “Something came up.” 드라마 속 바쁜 사장님 같았어요!

lines.en: Ha! I practiced that line. Sorry for the short notice, and thanks for being flexible.
lines.ko: 하하! 그 대사 연습했거든요. 갑자기 말해서 미안하고, 맞춰 줘서 고마워요.

lines.en: No problem. Good luck with the review!
lines.ko: 괜찮아요. 검토 회의 잘해요!

lines.en: Thanks. If anything changes, {{I’ll keep you posted}}.
lines.ko: 고마워요. 뭐라도 바뀌면 알려 줄게요.

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "A Change of Plans · 9월 말 목요일, 전화 통화", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Chloe: "Hi, Jiwoo! Are we still on for lunch tomorrow? I found a great new noodle place." (지우 씨, 안녕하세요! 내일 점심 약속 그대로죠? 새로 생긴 좋은 국숫집을 찾았어요.)
2. Jiwoo: "Hi, Chloe. I’m so sorry, but something came up. We have an urgent design review tomorrow." (안녕하세요, 클로이 씨. 정말 미안한데, 일이 좀 생겼어요. 내일 급한 디자인 검토 회의가 있어요.)
3. Chloe: "Oh no. On a Friday?" (저런. 금요일에요?)
4. Jiwoo: "Yes. The Vancouver team needs our new screens soon, and we’re a bit behind schedule." (네. 밴쿠버 팀이 새 화면을 곧 받아야 하는데, 저희가 일정보다 좀 늦어졌어요.)
5. Chloe: "That sounds stressful. Don’t worry about lunch." (스트레스받겠네요. 점심은 걱정하지 마요.)
6. Jiwoo: "Thanks. Could we push it back to next week? Maybe Monday?" (고마워요. 다음 주로 미룰 수 있을까요? 월요일 어때요?)
7. Chloe: "Hmm, Monday clashes with a video shoot. Would Tuesday suit you better?" (음, 월요일은 영상 촬영이랑 겹쳐요. 화요일이 더 괜찮아요?)
8. Jiwoo: "Tuesday works for me. Same time, twelve thirty?" (화요일 좋아요. 같은 시간, 12시 반이요?)
9. Chloe: "Perfect. Ooh, by the way, “Something came up.” You sounded like a busy boss in a TV drama!" (좋아요. 아, 그런데 “Something came up.” 드라마 속 바쁜 사장님 같았어요!)
10. Jiwoo: "Ha! I practiced that line. Sorry for the short notice, and thanks for being flexible." (하하! 그 대사 연습했거든요. 갑자기 말해서 미안하고, 맞춰 줘서 고마워요.)
11. Chloe: "No problem. Good luck with the review!" (괜찮아요. 검토 회의 잘해요!)
12. Jiwoo: "Thanks. If anything changes, I’ll keep you posted." (고마워요. 뭐라도 바뀌면 알려 줄게요.)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. The learner plays Jiwoo in this lesson, so an answer in the first person (I'm new here instead of Jiwoo is new here) is right too; never correct that. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

First say in one short sentence that they will be Jiwoo and you will read Chloe. Then go in order, one line at a time: call highlight_line with the line number before each line, read your line, and for the learner's line just wait for them to say it. If they say most of it or a good part of a long line, accept it warmly and go on; only if what they say is clearly not their line, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, give one short warm comment on how they did, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick true/false check about the scene.

frame: Something came up. Could we push it back to ___?
Would ___ suit you better? / Works for me.
head: 약속
이유 (Something came up.)
새 시간 (push it back to …)
rows: My last meeting is running late.
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: Something came up. Could we push it back to ___? / Would ___ suit you better? / Works for me. Table (약속 → 이유 (Something came up.)):
- lunch on Friday → We have an urgent review.
- our 3 p.m. meeting → My last meeting is running late.
- our call → My flight was delayed.
- the dinner party → I have to work late.
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items: push back · move forward — it은 가운데

Could we *push* it *back* to Tuesday? 늦추다 
Can we *move* it *forward*? 앞당기다 
it·them은 가운데에 넣어요: push *it* back

Something *came up*. 갑자기 일이 생겼어요.(come → came) 
A problem came up at work. (목적어 없이 써요) 
I’ll *keep* you *posted*. keep + 사람 + posted
errors: Could we push back it to Tuesday?
Could we push it back to Tuesday?
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- push back · move forward — it은 가운데: Could we push it back to Tuesday? 늦추다 / Can we move it forward? 앞당기다 / it·them은 가운데에 넣어요: push it back
- come up · keep you posted: Something came up. 갑자기 일이 생겼어요.(come → came) / A problem came up at work. (목적어 없이 써요) / I’ll keep you posted. keep + 사람 + posted
Common mistakes on screen:
- Could we push back it to Tuesday? → Could we push it back to Tuesday? (it은 push와 back 사이에.)
- Something comes up yesterday. → Something came up yesterday. (지난 일이라 came.)
- I’ll keep you post. → I’ll keep you posted. (keep you 뒤에는 posted.)
- Sorry for the short notify. → Sorry for the short notice. (for 뒤에는 명사 notice.)
There are 2 grammar points and 4 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

come up · keep you posted: Something came up. 갑자기 일이 생겼어요.(come → came) A problem came up at work. (목적어 없이 써요) I’ll keep you posted. keep + 사람 + posted

steps.note: 예) Friday lunch / next Tuesday → Something came up. Could we push it back to next Tuesday? — Sure. Works for me.
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) Friday lunch / next Tuesday → Something came up. Could we push it back to next Tuesday? — Sure. Works for me. The items (the words the learner gets for each one): Friday lunch / next Tuesday | the 3 p.m. meeting / four thirty | our call / tomorrow morning | the design review / Thursday.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

cards: Could we push it back to ___?
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "Could we push it back?" (일정 미루기); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "Could we push it back to ___?" / "Something came up." / "I’ll keep you posted.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: I’m afraid I need to reschedule.
I’ll get back to you by Friday.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 일정 바꾸자고 하기: "I’m afraid I need to reschedule." (죄송하지만 일정을 다시 잡아야겠어요., 정중); "Sorry for the short notice." (갑자기 말씀드려 죄송해요., 정중); "We’re a bit behind schedule." (일정보다 좀 늦어졌어요., 보통); "Can we move it forward?" (좀 앞당길 수 있을까요?, 보통)
- 새 시간 정하기: "Would ___ suit you better?" (~가 더 괜찮으세요?, 정중); "Works for me." (저는 좋아요., 친근); "Thanks for being flexible." (맞춰 줘서 고마워요., 보통)
- 계속 연락하기: "Let’s touch base on ___." (~에 잠깐 이야기 나눠요., 보통); "I’ll get back to you by Friday." (금요일까지 답을 드릴게요., 보통)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

Tips on screen:

items.ko: (일정 등을) 바꿀 수 있는, 융통성 있는

steps.teach:
Picture words on screen. New: reschedule (일정을 다시 잡다), timeline ((날짜별) 진행 일정표), time slot ((정해진) 시간대), clash ((시간이) 겹치다), progress (진행, 진척), status ((지금의) 상황, 상태), submit (제출하다), extend (늘리다, 연장하다), notice ((미리 하는) 통보, 알림), flexible ((일정 등을) 바꿀 수 있는, 융통성 있는), ahead (앞에; 미리), arrangement ((함께 정한) 약속, 준비).
Go through about six, new ones first, one word per turn: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and wait for the learner to say it before the next word. Never give several words in one turn. After every two or three words, ask one tiny real question with the word you just did (for example: Are you a morning person?), wait for the answer and react; do this at least twice in this part. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

Word list on screen: suit ((시간 등이) ~에게 맞다) — "Would Tuesday suit you?"; commit ((~하기로) 약속하다) — "I can’t commit to Friday."; postpone (미루다, 연기하다) — "Let’s postpone the lunch."; deadline (마감(일)) — "The deadline is Monday."; behind ((예정보다) 늦은, 뒤처진) — "We’re behind schedule."; schedule (일정) — "a busy schedule"; extension ((기한) 연장) — "Can I get an extension?"; delay (늦추다, 지연시키다; 지연) — "My flight was delayed."; update (새 소식, 최신 정보) — "a quick status update".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.

- "A friend wants to meet on Friday, but you’re busy. What do you say?" (hint on screen: Something came up. Could we push it back to ___?)

Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.

steps.title: Lunch on Tuesday
steps.text: On Tuesday at twelve thirty, Jiwoo finally met Chloe at a small noodle restaurant near Jiwoo’s office. “So, how did the review go?” Chloe asked. “Initially, it was stressful,” said Jiwoo. “Work was mounting up. But the review *in itself* was helpful. I *put forward* some newly designed icons, and the team liked them.” She explained that the Vancouver team had *laid down* a clear timeline. *To date*, they’ve finished the first sequence of screens. The subsequent screens are due at the end of October, *subject to* change. “It’s hard to *keep up* sometimes,” she admitted. Chloe smiled. “*In short*, you’re busy but happy.” “Exactly. And I’m not scared of video meetings anymore,” said Jiwoo. “Stay tuned!”
steps.gloss: initially 처음에는 · in itself 그 자체로는 · put forward 내놓다, 제안하다 · lay down (계획을) 정하다 · to date 지금까지 · sequence (차례로 이어진) 한 묶음 · subsequent 그다음의 · subject to change 바뀔 수 있는 · keep up 뒤처지지 않고 따라가다
questions: What did the Vancouver team lay down?
When are the subsequent screens due?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "Lunch on Tuesday". Text: "On Tuesday at twelve thirty, Jiwoo finally met Chloe at a small noodle restaurant near Jiwoo’s office. “So, how did the review go?” Chloe asked. “Initially, it was stressful,” said Jiwoo. “Work was mounting up. But the review in itself was helpful. I put forward some newly designed icons, and the team liked them.” She explained that the Vancouver team had laid down a clear timeline. steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.

Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "It must be something for plants." (뭘까요? 추측하기). Goal: 확신 정도에 따라 추측하고(must·might), 의심을 말하기. steps.when: 단서가 확실할 때 강하게 추측해요.

steps.title: The Box with No Name · 10월 첫 토요일, 1층 우편함 앞에서

lines.en: Morning, Jiwoo. Have you seen this big box? It’s been sitting here since Wednesday.
lines.ko: 좋은 아침이에요, 지우 씨. 이 큰 상자 봤어요? 수요일부터 여기 있었어요.

lines.en: Yes! There’s no name on it, just a wet label with a “5” on it.
lines.ko: 네! 이름은 없고, ‘5’라고 적힌 젖은 라벨만 있어요.

lines.en: The fifth floor? Then {{it might be}} yours.
lines.ko: 5층이요? 그럼 지우 씨 거일지도 몰라요.

lines.en: {{I doubt it.}} I haven’t ordered anything this week.
lines.ko: 아닐 거예요. 이번 주엔 아무것도 주문 안 했어요.

lines.en: Okay, let’s look for clues. It’s big, but it’s really light.
lines.ko: 좋아요, 단서를 찾아봐요. 크긴 한데 정말 가벼워요.

lines.en: So it can’t be books. And look, this side has collapsed a little. Something round is inside.
lines.ko: 그럼 책일 리는 없어요. 봐요, 이쪽이 조금 찌그러졌어요. 안에 둥근 게 있어요.

lines.en: Round and light… It could be a big plate?
lines.ko: 둥글고 가볍고… 큰 접시일 수도 있겠네요?

lines.en: Wait, there’s a trace of soil on the corner. {{It must be}} something for plants!
lines.ko: 잠깐, 모서리에 흙이 조금 묻어 있어요. 분명 식물에 쓰는 물건일 거예요!

lines.en: Plants on the fifth floor? I bet it’s Grace’s. Her place is like a little forest.
lines.ko: 5층에 식물이라면? 그레이스 거가 틀림없어요. 그 집은 작은 숲 같잖아요.

lines.en: You’re right! I’m pretty sure she said she needed new saucers for her pots.
lines.ko: 맞아요! 화분 받침이 새로 필요하다고 했던 게 거의 확실해요.

lines.en: Let’s find out. I’ll text her. If we’re wrong, I’ll knock on every door on the fifth floor!
lines.ko: 확인해 봐요. 제가 문자 보낼게요. 틀리면 5층 문을 다 두드려 볼게요!

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "The Box with No Name · 10월 첫 토요일, 1층 우편함 앞에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Ben: "Morning, Jiwoo. Have you seen this big box? It’s been sitting here since Wednesday." (좋은 아침이에요, 지우 씨. 이 큰 상자 봤어요? 수요일부터 여기 있었어요.)
2. Jiwoo: "Yes! There’s no name on it, just a wet label with a “5” on it." (네! 이름은 없고, ‘5’라고 적힌 젖은 라벨만 있어요.)
3. Ben: "The fifth floor? Then it might be yours." (5층이요? 그럼 지우 씨 거일지도 몰라요.)
4. Jiwoo: "I doubt it. I haven’t ordered anything this week." (아닐 거예요. 이번 주엔 아무것도 주문 안 했어요.)
5. Ben: "Okay, let’s look for clues. It’s big, but it’s really light." (좋아요, 단서를 찾아봐요. 크긴 한데 정말 가벼워요.)
6. Jiwoo: "So it can’t be books. And look, this side has collapsed a little. Something round is inside." (그럼 책일 리는 없어요. 봐요, 이쪽이 조금 찌그러졌어요. 안에 둥근 게 있어요.)
7. Ben: "Round and light… It could be a big plate?" (둥글고 가볍고… 큰 접시일 수도 있겠네요?)
8. Jiwoo: "Wait, there’s a trace of soil on the corner. It must be something for plants!" (잠깐, 모서리에 흙이 조금 묻어 있어요. 분명 식물에 쓰는 물건일 거예요!)
9. Ben: "Plants on the fifth floor? I bet it’s Grace’s. Her place is like a little forest." (5층에 식물이라면? 그레이스 거가 틀림없어요. 그 집은 작은 숲 같잖아요.)
10. Jiwoo: "You’re right! I’m pretty sure she said she needed new saucers for her pots." (맞아요! 화분 받침이 새로 필요하다고 했던 게 거의 확실해요.)
11. Ben: "Let’s find out. I’ll text her. If we’re wrong, I’ll knock on every door on the fifth floor!" (확인해 봐요. 제가 문자 보낼게요. 틀리면 5층 문을 다 두드려 볼게요!)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. The learner plays Jiwoo in this lesson, so an answer in the first person (I'm new here instead of Jiwoo is new here) is right too; never correct that. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.
