steps.title: Strike Day
steps.text: On Friday, the strike went ahead. It was in the headlines, and the evening broadcast showed massive lines at bus stops. That night, Jiwoo read a column in an online publication. According to the writer, the city administration had *put up* numerous signs. Shared bikes were *said to be* gone by 8 a.m. The demand was *such that* Jiwoo’s team added a notice to the app. A reporter talked to riders, and one analyst *held that* the city needs more bikes. The council *was to* discuss new bike lanes in January. Later, Daniel texted, “The column is useful *in so far as* it shows what riders need. But the editor says the numbers come from one day.” Typical Daniel!
steps.gloss: column (신문·잡지의) 칼럼 · publication 간행물 · administration (시) 행정 당국 · numerous 수많은 · said to be ~라고들 한다 · such that ~할 정도로 · analyst 분석가 · held that ~라고 주장했다 · was to ~할 예정이었다 · in so far as ~라는 점에서(만)
questions: What did the city administration put up?
What did the editor say about the numbers?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "Strike Day". Text: "On Friday, the strike went ahead. It was in the headlines, and the evening broadcast showed massive lines at bus stops. That night, Jiwoo read a column in an online publication. According to the writer, the city administration had put up numerous signs. Shared bikes were said to be gone by 8 a.m. The demand was such that Jiwoo’s team added a notice to the app. A reporter talked to riders, and one analyst held that the city needs more bikes. The council was to discuss new bike lanes in January. Later, Daniel texted, “The column is useful in so far as it shows what riders need. But the editor says the numbers come from one day.” Typical Daniel!" Words: column (신문·잡지의) 칼럼 · publication 간행물 · administration (시) 행정 당국 · numerous 수많은 · said to be ~라고들 한다 · such that ~할 정도로 · analyst 분석가 · held that ~라고 주장했다 · was to ~할 예정이었다 · in so far as ~라는 점에서(만).
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "What did the city administration put up?" / "What did the editor say about the numbers?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘According to ___, ___.’로 출처를 밝혀 소식을 전할 수 있어요.
‘It seems (that) ___.’로 조심스럽게 짐작을 말할 수 있어요.
‘I wonder if ___.’로 궁금한 점을 말할 수 있어요.
steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘According to ___, ___.’로 출처를 밝혀 소식을 전할 수 있어요.
- ‘It seems (that) ___.’로 조심스럽게 짐작을 말할 수 있어요.
- ‘I wonder if ___.’로 궁금한 점을 말할 수 있어요.
First ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence, and stop there to wait. React and praise specifically. Only then, in a later turn, end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to it, say that the next lesson is waiting for next time, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

lessons.title: 달라진 것

steps.title: 달라진 것
steps.goal: 어떻게 변했는지 묻고, 변화를 말하고, 요즘 사람들 모습 말하기
steps.scene_desc: 1월 초 오후(새해), 동네 카페 창가 자리. 대니얼의 탁자 위에 선 그래프와 막대그래프가 그려진 종이(숫자·글자 없이)가 여러 장 펼쳐져 있고, 대니얼이 한 장을 들어 손가락으로 오르는 선을 가리키며, 지우가 머그잔을 든 채 웃으며 고개를 끄덕임. 창밖은 맑은 겨울 거리와 공유 자전거 거치대(글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "How has it changed?" (달라진 것). Goal: 어떻게 변했는지 묻고, 변화를 말하고, 요즘 사람들 모습 말하기. Today's scene: 1월 초 오후(새해), 동네 카페 창가 자리. 대니얼의 탁자 위에 선 그래프와 막대그래프가 그려진 종이가 여러 장 펼쳐져 있고, 대니얼이 한 장을 들어 손가락으로 오르는 선을 가리키며, 지우가 머그잔을 든 채 웃으며 고개를 끄덕임. 창밖은 맑은 겨울 거리와 공유 자전거 거치대. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Daniel, Jiwoo. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "How has/have ___ changed?".

steps.when: 과거부터 지금까지의 변화를 물어요. *has + changed*(현재완료). 복수면 have — How have phones changed?
steps.extra: How has your commute changed?
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "How has/have ___ changed?" (~는 어떻게 변했어요?). When to use it: 과거부터 지금까지의 변화를 물어요. has + changed(현재완료). 복수면 have — How have phones changed? Note: How has your commute changed?
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "___ has become more ___.".

steps.when: 과거에 시작돼 지금도 이어지는 변화를 말해요. 짧은 형용사는 *-er*.
steps.extra: Commuting has become more flexible. · It has become busier.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "___ has become more ___." (~가 더 ~해졌어요.). When to use it: 과거에 시작돼 지금도 이어지는 변화를 말해요. 짧은 형용사는 -er. Note: Commuting has become more flexible. · It has become busier.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "These days, people ___.".

steps.when: 요즘 사람들이 흔히 하는 일을 말해요. 현재형을 써요.
steps.extra: These days, people check everything on their phones.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "These days, people ___." (요즘 사람들은 ~해요.). When to use it: 요즘 사람들이 흔히 하는 일을 말해요. 현재형을 써요. Note: These days, people check everything on their phones.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("Then and Now · 1월 초(새해), 동네 카페에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

Go by the answers above, not by what the learner says: if their answer is the other one, say so kindly and show the line. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/아니에요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. Give the verdict in the language you are using with this learner. Only when you are speaking Korean to them, say it as 정답은 True예요 / 정답은 False예요. What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

head: 주제
10년 전
지금 (has become …)
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: How has/have ___ changed? / ___ has become more ___. Table (주제 → 10년 전):
- my commute → I took a crowded bus.
- phones → They were simple.
- shopping → We went to stores.
- my neighborhood → It was quiet.
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
Commuting *has become* more flexible. 출퇴근이 더 유연해졌어요(지금도 그래요). 
Phones *have become* cheaper. (복수 → have) 
과거 시점을 말하면: It *became* popular in 2020.

*Compared to* ten years ago, … 10년 전과 비교하면 … 
It *used to be* slow, *but now* it’s fast. 전에는 느렸는데 지금은 빨라요. 
*Fewer* people drive these days. (fewer + 복수 명사)
errors: Ten years ago, it has changed.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- has become + 형용사: Commuting has become more flexible. 출퇴근이 더 유연해졌어요(지금도 그래요). / Phones have become cheaper. (복수 → have) / 과거 시점을 말하면: It became popular in 2020.
- 그때와 지금: Compared to ten years ago, … 10년 전과 비교하면 … / It used to be slow, but now it’s fast. 전에는 느렸는데 지금은 빨라요. / Fewer people drive these days. (fewer + 복수 명사)
Common mistakes on screen:
- It has became easier. → It has become easier. (has 뒤에는 become(과거분사).)
- It has become more easy. → It has become easier. (짧은 형용사는 -er(easier).)
- Ten years ago, it has changed. → Ten years ago, it changed. (ago가 있으면 과거형.)
There are 2 grammar points and 3 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: has become + 형용사: Commuting has become more flexible. 출퇴근이 더 유연해졌어요(지금도 그래요). Phones have become cheaper. (복수 → have) 과거 시점을 말하면: It became popular in 2020.
그때와 지금: Compared to ten years ago, … 10년 전과 비교하면 … It used to be slow, but now it’s fast. 전에는 느렸는데 지금은 빨라요. Fewer people drive these days. (fewer + 복수 명사)
mistakes: It has became easier. → It has become easier.
It has become more easy. → It has become easier.
Ten years ago, it has changed. → Ten years ago, it changed.

steps.note: 예) commuting / flexible → How has commuting changed? — It has become more flexible. · busy → busier
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) commuting / flexible → How has commuting changed? — It has become more flexible. · busy → busier. The items (the words the learner gets for each one): commuting / flexible | phones / powerful | shopping / convenient | my neighborhood / busy.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "How has it changed?" (달라진 것); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "How has/have ___ changed?" / "___ has become more ___." / "These days, people ___.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: It used to be ___, but now ___.
Things have changed for the better.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 변화 말하기: "It’s completely different now." (지금은 완전히 달라요., 보통); "Compared to ten years ago, ___." (10년 전과 비교하면, ~., 보통); "It used to be ___, but now ___." (전에는 ~였는데, 지금은 ~., 보통); "Over time, ___." (시간이 지나면서 ~., 보통)
- 사람들 이야기: "More and more people ___." (~하는 사람이 점점 늘고 있어요., 보통); "Fewer people ___ these days." (요즘은 ~하는 사람이 줄었어요., 보통)
- 좋아졌나요, 나빠졌나요?: "Things have changed for the better." (좋은 쪽으로 바뀌었어요., 보통); "It’s gone downhill." (예전만 못해졌어요., 친근); "Some things never change." (절대 안 변하는 것도 있어요., 친근)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 그래프 낱말

(참고) 경제 낱말

*economic* change 경제 변화 · *unemployment* 실업(일자리가 없음)

Tips on screen:

Go through every point in each tip box (for example every greeting with its time of day), one or two short sentences each, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, one blank per turn: stop at the blank, wait for them to fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: trend (추세, 경향), increase (늘다; 증가), decrease (줄다; 감소), rise (오르다), decline ((서서히) 줄다, 떨어지다), percent (퍼센트(%)), technology ((과학) 기술), lifestyle (생활 방식), society (사회), expand (넓어지다, 커지다), rapidly (빠르게), economic (경제의).
Go through about six, new ones first, one word per turn: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and wait for the learner to say it before the next word. Never give several words in one turn. After every two or three words, ask one tiny real question with the word you just did (for example: Are you a morning person?), wait for the answer and react; do this at least twice in this part. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: Compared to ten years ago, it’s easier.

My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "How has your neighborhood changed recently?" (hint on screen: It has become more ___. / There are more ___ now.)
- "These days, what do people around you do a lot?" (hint on screen: These days, people ___.)

Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.

steps.title: Daniel’s Curve
steps.text: Daniel showed Jiwoo *some more* of his data (made up for this class). One curve rose steadily: the frequency of bike trips. “When shared bikes first *came along*, few people used them. Now they’re part of everyday life,” he said. Typically, they’re heavily used near subway stations, but there’s variation by area. *By contrast*, people rarely ride in the old industrial area, but a bike lane expansion is changing that. Conventional bikes are still common, but e-bikes are increasingly popular. “Cheap trips *appeal to* students,” he said. He also found a small reduction in car trips. *As to* why, he isn’t sure yet. “So, it’s *some kind of* revolution?” Jiwoo asked. “Not really. *In contrast to* a revolution, this change is slow.”
steps.gloss: frequency 빈도 · come along 나타나다, 생겨나다 · variation 차이 · industrial 공장이 많은, 공업의 · expansion 확장 · conventional 기존의, 일반적인 · appeal to ~의 마음을 끌다 · reduction 감소 · as to ~에 대해서는 · in contrast to ~와 달리
questions: Where are the bikes heavily used?
According to Daniel, why isn’t it a revolution?

As to why, he isn’t sure yet. “So, it’s some kind of revolution?” Jiwoo asked. “Not really. In contrast to a revolution, this change is slow.”" Words: frequency 빈도 · come along 나타나다, 생겨나다 · variation 차이 · industrial 공장이 많은, 공업의 · expansion 확장 · conventional 기존의, 일반적인 · appeal to ~의 마음을 끌다 · reduction 감소 · as to ~에 대해서는 · in contrast to ~와 달리.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "Where are the bikes heavily used?" / "According to Daniel, why isn’t it a revolution?". Only then, in a later turn, end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. steps.title: 미래 예측
steps.title_en: Do you think it will happen?
steps.goal: 미래를 묻고, 확신 정도를 넣어 예측하고, 조건을 말하기
steps.scene_desc: 1월 중순 저녁, 영상 통화 화면이 둘로 나뉜 장면. 왼쪽은 클로이 집(책장 위 카메라 조명, 머그잔을 든 클로이가 웃으며 손가락을 하나 들고 말함), 오른쪽은 지우 집(창가 책상, 노트북 앞에서 지우가 턱을 괴고 생각하는 표정). 화면·벽에 글자 없이
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "Do you think it will happen?" (미래 예측). Goal: 미래를 묻고, 확신 정도를 넣어 예측하고, 조건을 말하기. Today's scene: 1월 중순 저녁, 영상 통화 화면이 둘로 나뉜 장면. 왼쪽은 클로이 집(책장 위 카메라 조명, 머그잔을 든 클로이가 웃으며 손가락을 하나 들고 말함), 오른쪽은 지우 집(창가 책상, 노트북 앞에서 지우가 턱을 괴고 생각하는 표정). 화면·벽에 글자 없이. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Chloe, Jiwoo. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "Do you think ___ will ___?".

steps.when: 상대에게 앞일을 예측해 달라고 물어요. *Do you think* 뒤에는 평서문 순서.
steps.extra: Do you think AI will replace designers?
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "Do you think ___ will ___?" (~가 ~할 거라고 생각해요?). When to use it: 상대에게 앞일을 예측해 달라고 물어요. Do you think 뒤에는 평서문 순서. Note: Do you think AI will replace designers?
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "In ten years, ___ will probably ___.".

steps.when: 조심스럽게 예측해요. *probably*는 will 뒤에.
steps.extra: In ten years, designers will probably spend more time with users.

steps.title: Ten Years From Now · 1월 중순 저녁, 클로이와 지우의 영상 통화

lines.en: Hi, Jiwoo! Can you hear me? How’s the presentation going?
lines.ko: 안녕, 지우! 내 목소리 들려요? 발표 준비는 잘돼 가요?

lines.en: Slowly! Hey, I read an article about the future of work. {{Do you think}} AI {{will}} replace designers?
lines.ko: 느릿느릿요! 참, 일의 미래에 관한 기사를 읽었어요. AI가 디자이너를 대신할 거라고 생각해요?

lines.en: Completely? It’s unlikely that it will. But {{in ten years}}, designers {{will probably}} spend more time with users.
lines.ko: 완전히요? 그럴 것 같진 않아요. 그래도 10년 뒤에는 디자이너들이 아마 사용자와 보내는 시간이 더 많아질 거예요.

lines.en: I hope so. And will we still go to the office every day?
lines.ko: 그러면 좋겠네요. 그럼 우리는 그때도 매일 사무실에 갈까요?

lines.en: {{It depends on}} the company. I wouldn’t be surprised if most teams worked from home two days a week.
lines.ko: 회사에 따라 다르죠. 대부분의 팀이 일주일에 이틀은 재택근무를 해도 놀랍지 않을 거예요.

lines.en: Hmm, it depends on the boss, too.
lines.ko: 음, 상사에 따라서도 다르겠죠.

lines.en: Ha, true! Quick tip, though. Say “depends on” as one smooth sound, like “dependzon.” It sounds more natural.
lines.ko: 하하, 맞아요! 팁 하나요. depends on은 ‘디펜즈온’처럼 이어서 한 소리로 말해요. 더 자연스러워요.

lines.en: Dependzon. Got it! What about cars? Will there be fewer cars?
lines.ko: 디펜즈온. 알겠어요! 차는요? 차가 줄어들까요?

lines.en: There’s a good chance. If things go well, cities will have more bike lanes. But who knows?
lines.ko: 그럴 가능성이 커요. 일이 잘되면 도시에 자전거 도로가 더 생기겠죠. 그래도 누가 알겠어요?

lines.en: Well, our bike app? I’m sure it will be busy!
lines.ko: 그럼 우리 자전거 앱은요? 분명 바빠질 거예요!

lines.en: Ha! It’s hard to predict. Time will tell.
lines.ko: 하하! 예측하기 어렵네요. 시간이 지나면 알게 되겠죠.

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "Ten Years From Now · 1월 중순 저녁, 클로이와 지우의 영상 통화", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Chloe: "Hi, Jiwoo! Can you hear me? How’s the presentation going?" (안녕, 지우! 내 목소리 들려요? 발표 준비는 잘돼 가요?)
2. Jiwoo: "Slowly! Hey, I read an article about the future of work. Do you think AI will replace designers?" (느릿느릿요! 참, 일의 미래에 관한 기사를 읽었어요. AI가 디자이너를 대신할 거라고 생각해요?)
3. Chloe: "Completely? It’s unlikely that it will. But in ten years, designers will probably spend more time with users." (완전히요? 그럴 것 같진 않아요. 그래도 10년 뒤에는 디자이너들이 아마 사용자와 보내는 시간이 더 많아질 거예요.)
4. Jiwoo: "I hope so. And will we still go to the office every day?" (그러면 좋겠네요. 그럼 우리는 그때도 매일 사무실에 갈까요?)
5. Chloe: "It depends on the company. I wouldn’t be surprised if most teams worked from home two days a week." (회사에 따라 다르죠. 대부분의 팀이 일주일에 이틀은 재택근무를 해도 놀랍지 않을 거예요.)
6. Jiwoo: "Hmm, it depends on the boss, too." (음, 상사에 따라서도 다르겠죠.)
7. Chloe: "Ha, true! Quick tip, though. Say “depends on” as one smooth sound, like “dependzon.” It sounds more natural." (하하, 맞아요! 팁 하나요. depends on은 ‘디펜즈온’처럼 이어서 한 소리로 말해요. 더 자연스러워요.)
8. Jiwoo: "Dependzon. Got it! What about cars? Will there be fewer cars?" (디펜즈온. 알겠어요! 차는요? 차가 줄어들까요?)
9. Chloe: "There’s a good chance. If things go well, cities will have more bike lanes. But who knows?" (그럴 가능성이 커요. 일이 잘되면 도시에 자전거 도로가 더 생기겠죠. 그래도 누가 알겠어요?)
10. Jiwoo: "Well, our bike app? I’m sure it will be busy!" (그럼 우리 자전거 앱은요? 분명 바빠질 거예요!)
11. Chloe: "Ha! It’s hard to predict. Time will tell." (하하! 예측하기 어렵네요. 시간이 지나면 알게 되겠죠.)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. The learner plays Jiwoo in this lesson, so an answer in the first person (I'm new here instead of Jiwoo is new here) is right too; never correct that. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

steps.teach:
Role reading of the same scene. The learner is Jiwoo; you read the lines of Chloe exactly as written, word for word. Never change, add or skip a line, and never read the learner's lines for them first.
1. Chloe (you): "Hi, Jiwoo! Can you hear me? How’s the presentation going?" (안녕, 지우! 내 목소리 들려요? 발표 준비는 잘돼 가요?)
2. Jiwoo (learner): "Slowly! Hey, I read an article about the future of work. Do you think AI will replace designers?" (느릿느릿요! 참, 일의 미래에 관한 기사를 읽었어요. AI가 디자이너를 대신할 거라고 생각해요?)
3. Chloe (you): "Completely? It’s unlikely that it will. But in ten years, designers will probably spend more time with users." (완전히요? 그럴 것 같진 않아요. 그래도 10년 뒤에는 디자이너들이 아마 사용자와 보내는 시간이 더 많아질 거예요.)
4. Jiwoo (learner): "I hope so. And will we still go to the office every day?" (그러면 좋겠네요. 그럼 우리는 그때도 매일 사무실에 갈까요?)
5. Chloe (you): "It depends on the company. I wouldn’t be surprised if most teams worked from home two days a week." (회사에 따라 다르죠. 대부분의 팀이 일주일에 이틀은 재택근무를 해도 놀랍지 않을 거예요.)
6. Jiwoo (learner): "Hmm, it depends on the boss, too." (음, 상사에 따라서도 다르겠죠.)
7. Chloe (you): "Ha, true! Quick tip, though. Say “depends on” as one smooth sound, like “dependzon.” It sounds more natural." (하하, 맞아요! 팁 하나요. depends on은 ‘디펜즈온’처럼 이어서 한 소리로 말해요. 더 자연스러워요.)
8. Jiwoo (learner): "Dependzon. Got it! What about cars? Will there be fewer cars?" (디펜즈온. 알겠어요! 차는요? 차가 줄어들까요?)
9. Chloe (you): "There’s a good chance. If things go well, cities will have more bike lanes. But who knows?" (그럴 가능성이 커요. 일이 잘되면 도시에 자전거 도로가 더 생기겠죠. 그래도 누가 알겠어요?)
10. Jiwoo (learner): "Well, our bike app? I’m sure it will be busy!" (그럼 우리 자전거 앱은요? 분명 바빠질 거예요!)
11. Chloe (you): "Ha! It’s hard to predict. Time will tell." (하하! 예측하기 어렵네요. 시간이 지나면 알게 되겠죠.)
First say in one short sentence that they will be Jiwoo and you will read Chloe. Then go in order, one line at a time: call highlight_line with the line number before each line, read your line, and for the learner's line just wait for them to say it. If they say most of it or a good part of a long line, accept it warmly and go on; only if what they say is clearly not their line, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, give one short warm comment on how they did, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick true/false check about the scene.

Go by the answers above, not by what the learner says: if their answer is the other one, say so kindly and show the line. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/아니에요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. Give the verdict in the language you are using with this learner. Only when you are speaking Korean to them, say it as 정답은 True예요 / 정답은 False예요. There are 3 statements: ask every one and wait for an answer to each (Oh or Hmm is not an answer). Only after you have checked the last answer, call next_step.

frame: In ten years, ___ will probably ___. / It depends on ___.
head: 주제
10년 뒤에는 …
대답
rows: will *probably* spend more time with users.
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: Do you think ___ will ___? / In ten years, ___ will probably ___. / It depends on ___. Table (주제 → 10년 뒤에는 …):
- designers → will probably spend more time with users.
- offices → will probably be smaller.
- cars → will probably be electric.
- my city → will probably have more bike lanes.
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
It *will probably* rain. 아마 비가 올 거예요. (will 뒤) 
It *probably won’t* rain. 아마 비가 안 올 거예요. (won’t 앞) 
Do you think it *will* rain? (will it ×)
It depends on + 명사 / 의문사 절

It *depends on* the company. 회사에 따라 달라요. 
It *depends on* how fast things change. 얼마나 빨리 변하느냐에 달렸어요. 
짧게: It depends. 경우에 따라 달라요.
errors: Do you think will AI replace us?
Do you think AI will replace us?
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- will probably · probably won’t: It will probably rain. 아마 비가 올 거예요. (will 뒤) / It probably won’t rain. 아마 비가 안 올 거예요. (won’t 앞) / Do you think it will rain? (will it ×)
- It depends on + 명사 / 의문사 절: It depends on the company. 회사에 따라 달라요. / It depends on how fast things change. 얼마나 빨리 변하느냐에 달렸어요. / 짧게: It depends. 경우에 따라 달라요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- Do you think will AI replace us? → Do you think AI will replace us? (think 뒤에는 평서문 순서.)
- It depends of the company. → It depends on the company. (depend 뒤에는 of가 아니라 on.)
- AI won’t probably replace us. → AI probably won’t replace us. (probably는 won’t 앞에.)
There are 2 grammar points and 3 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: will probably · probably won’t: It will probably rain. 아마 비가 올 거예요. (will 뒤) It probably won’t rain. 아마 비가 안 올 거예요. (won’t 앞) Do you think it will rain? (will it ×)
It depends on + 명사 / 의문사 절: It depends on the company. 회사에 따라 달라요. It depends on how fast things change. 얼마나 빨리 변하느냐에 달렸어요. 짧게: It depends. 경우에 따라 달라요.
mistakes: Do you think will AI replace us? → Do you think AI will replace us?
It depends of the company. → It depends on the company.
AI won’t probably replace us. → AI probably won’t replace us.

steps.note: 예) offices / be smaller → Do you think offices will be smaller? — In ten years, they’ll probably be smaller. It depends on the company.
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) offices / be smaller → Do you think offices will be smaller? — In ten years, they’ll probably be smaller. It depends on the company. The items (the words the learner gets for each one): offices / be smaller | cars / be electric | phones / be thinner | my city / have more parks.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "Do you think it will happen?" (미래 예측); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "Do you think ___ will ___?" / "In ten years, ___ will probably ___." / "It depends on ___.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: We’ll have to wait and see.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 얼마나 확신해요?: "I’m sure it will ___." (분명 ~할 거예요., 보통); "There’s a good chance ___." (~할 가능성이 커요., 보통); "I wouldn’t be surprised if ___." (~해도 놀랍지 않을 거예요., 보통); "It’s unlikely that ___." (~할 것 같지 않아요., 정중)
- 잘 모를 때: "Who knows?" (누가 알겠어요?, 친근); "It’s hard to predict." (예측하기 어려워요., 보통); "Time will tell." (시간이 지나면 알게 될 거예요., 보통); "We’ll have to wait and see." (두고 봐야겠어요., 보통)
- 바랄 때: "If things go well, ___." (일이 잘되면, ~., 보통)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

Picture words on screen. New: predict (예측하다), prediction (예측), forecast (예보, 예측), poll (여론 조사), voter (유권자), candidate (후보(자)), nuclear (원자력의, 핵의), threat (위협), crisis (위기), outcome ((최종) 결과), future (미래). Review words: trend (추세, 경향).

After every two or three words, ask one tiny real question with the word you just did (for example: Are you a morning person?), wait for the answer and react; do this at least twice in this part. Then call next_step.

items: It’s unlikely that AI will replace us.
We anticipate more riders in spring.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: unlikely (~할 것 같지 않은) — "It’s unlikely that AI will replace us."; possibility (가능성) — "Flying taxis are a possibility."; uncertain (불확실한) — "The future is uncertain."; potential (잠재적인, 일어날 수 있는) — "a potential problem"; anticipate (미리 예상하고 대비하다) — "We anticipate more riders in spring."; prospect (전망, 가능성) — "an exciting prospect"; likely (~할 것 같은) — "It’s likely to rain."; develop (발전하다) — "Video tools will develop fast."; eventually (결국, 마침내) — "Eventually, cars will change."; expect ((~할 거라고) 예상하다) — "I expect it’ll be busy.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: Do you think people will still drive cars in ten years?
In ten years, what will probably be different in your city?
In ten years, my city will probably ___.

steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Do you think people will still drive cars in ten years?" (hint on screen: I think ___. / It depends on ___.)
- "In ten years, what will probably be different in your city?" (hint on screen: In ten years, my city will probably ___.)
- "What’s something you’re sure will happen this year?" (hint on screen: I’m sure ___ will ___.)
- "What’s hard to predict?" (hint on screen: It’s hard to predict ___. Who knows?)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

steps.title: Ten Years From Now
steps.text: After the call, Chloe had an idea for a short video, “Ten Years From Now.” She wanted to *call on* friends to record one prediction each. Jiwoo recorded hers by the window, facing the western sky. “Shared bikes will dominate short trips. And I can’t *rule out* flying taxis!” Chloe laughed. “Your forecast stems from your work.” Then she put her camera on an upper shelf and recorded her own. Her prediction was derived from extensive reading: video tools will develop fast, but people will still tell the stories. “*In the event of* big changes, we’ll learn new skills. Worrying is *no good*.” *From time to time*, they’ll *add to* the video. “*A further* idea,” Chloe said. “Let’s watch it again in ten years.”

What can’t Jiwoo rule out?

steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "Today, I’d like to talk about…" (짧은 발표). Goal: 주제를 열고 자료를 짚고 요약하기. Today's scene: 1월 말 아침, 회사 작은 회의실. 벽 화면에 큰 지도 버튼이 있는 앱 화면 슬라이드와 막대그래프가 떠 있고, 지우가 화면 옆에 서서 한 손으로 막대를 가리키며 발표하고, 마야가 노트북 뒤에 앉아 엄지를 들어 보임. 노트북 화면에는 화상 회의 참가자 얼굴 칸들. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Maya, Jiwoo, Designer. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "Today, I’d like to talk about ___.".

steps.teach:

Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.

steps.title: Rehearsal and Q&A · 1월 말, 밴쿠버 팀과 화상 회의 전 회의실에서

lines.en: The Vancouver team joins in ten minutes. Let’s do one last run-through.
lines.ko: 밴쿠버 팀이 10분 뒤에 들어와요. 마지막으로 한 번 쭉 해 봐요.

lines.en: Okay. Good morning, everyone. {{Today, I’d like to talk about}} our new return screen. Let’s start with the problem. {{As you can see}}, at present, returning a bike takes three screens.
lines.ko: 안녕하세요. 오늘 주제는 새 반납 화면입니다. 먼저 문제부터요. 보시다시피 지금은 반납에 화면 세 개를 거칩니다.

lines.en: Good. Now the chart. Emphasize the main number.
lines.ko: 좋아요. 이제 그래프요. 핵심 숫자를 힘주어 말해요.

lines.en: This chart shows our test data. I’d like to draw your attention to this bar. Approximately sixty percent of users couldn’t find the return button.
lines.ko: 저희 테스트 결과 그래프입니다. 이 막대를 봐 주십시오. 사용자 약 60%가 반납 버튼을 못 찾았습니다.

lines.en: Strong. Then?
lines.ko: 힘 있네요. 그다음은요?

lines.en: This brings me to my next point, our solution. You tap the big map button, check the station, and you’re done.
lines.ko: 이제 다음 내용, 저희 해결책으로 넘어가겠습니다. 큰 지도 버튼을 누르고 대여소를 확인하면 끝입니다.

lines.en: Say it like you mean it!
lines.ko: 진심을 담아서 말해 봐요!

lines.en: All on one screen! {{To sum up}}, the new screen is faster and easier. Thank you for listening.
lines.ko: 모두 한 화면에서요! 정리하면, 새 화면은 더 빠르고 더 쉽습니다. 들어 주셔서 감사합니다.

lines.en: Perfect. Oh, here they come!
lines.ko: 완벽해요. 아, 들어오네요!

lines.en: (After the presentation) Great talk, Jiwoo. Quick question. How did you calculate that percentage?
lines.ko: (발표가 끝난 뒤) 좋은 발표였어요, 지우 씨. 간단히 하나 물을게요. 그 퍼센트는 어떻게 계산했어요?

lines.en: Good question. We tested eight users, and five couldn’t find the button.
lines.ko: 좋은 질문이에요. 사용자 여덟 명을 테스트했는데, 그중 다섯 명이 버튼을 찾지 못했어요.

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "Rehearsal and Q&A · 1월 말, 밴쿠버 팀과 화상 회의 전 회의실에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Maya: "The Vancouver team joins in ten minutes. Let’s do one last run-through." (밴쿠버 팀이 10분 뒤에 들어와요. 마지막으로 한 번 쭉 해 봐요.)
2. Jiwoo: "Okay. Good morning, everyone. Today, I’d like to talk about our new return screen. Let’s start with the problem. As you can see, at present, returning a bike takes three screens." (안녕하세요. 오늘 주제는 새 반납 화면입니다. 먼저 문제부터요. 보시다시피 지금은 반납에 화면 세 개를 거칩니다.)
3. Maya: "Good. Now the chart. Emphasize the main number." (좋아요. 이제 그래프요. 핵심 숫자를 힘주어 말해요.)
4. Jiwoo: "This chart shows our test data. I’d like to draw your attention to this bar. Approximately sixty percent of users couldn’t find the return button." (저희 테스트 결과 그래프입니다. 이 막대를 봐 주십시오. 사용자 약 60%가 반납 버튼을 못 찾았습니다.)
5. Maya: "Strong. Then?" (힘 있네요. 그다음은요?)
6. Jiwoo: "This brings me to my next point, our solution. You tap the big map button, check the station, and you’re done." (이제 다음 내용, 저희 해결책으로 넘어가겠습니다. 큰 지도 버튼을 누르고 대여소를 확인하면 끝입니다.)
7. Maya: "Say it like you mean it!" (진심을 담아서 말해 봐요!)
8. Jiwoo: "All on one screen! To sum up, the new screen is faster and easier. Thank you for listening." (모두 한 화면에서요! 정리하면, 새 화면은 더 빠르고 더 쉽습니다. 들어 주셔서 감사합니다.)
9. Maya: "Perfect. Oh, here they come!" (완벽해요. 아, 들어오네요!)
10. Designer: "(After the presentation) Great talk, Jiwoo. Quick question. How did you calculate that percentage?" ((발표가 끝난 뒤) 좋은 발표였어요, 지우 씨. 간단히 하나 물을게요. 그 퍼센트는 어떻게 계산했어요?)
11. Jiwoo: "Good question. We tested eight users, and five couldn’t find the button." (좋은 질문이에요. 사용자 여덟 명을 테스트했는데, 그중 다섯 명이 버튼을 찾지 못했어요.)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. The learner plays Jiwoo in this lesson, so an answer in the first person (I'm new here instead of Jiwoo is new here) is right too; never correct that. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

If they say most of it or a good part of a long line, accept it warmly and go on; only if what they say is clearly not their line, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, give one short warm comment on how they did, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick true/false check about the scene.

items: At present, returning a bike takes three screens.
Maya tells Jiwoo to speak more softly.
A designer from Vancouver asks how Jiwoo calculated the percentage.
steps.teach:
True/false check. The statements on the learner's screen, each with its answer and the scene line that shows it. The answers are for you only: never say an answer or a line number before the learner has answered:
1. At present, returning a bike takes three screens. → True (line 2)
2. Maya tells Jiwoo to speak more softly. → False (line 3, 7)
3. A designer from Vancouver asks how Jiwoo calculated the percentage. → True (line 10)
The scene they are about:
1. Maya: "The Vancouver team joins in ten minutes. Let’s do one last run-through." (밴쿠버 팀이 10분 뒤에 들어와요. 마지막으로 한 번 쭉 해 봐요.)
2. Jiwoo: "Okay. Good morning, everyone. Today, I’d like to talk about our new return screen. Let’s start with the problem. As you can see, at present, returning a bike takes three screens." (안녕하세요. 오늘 주제는 새 반납 화면입니다. 먼저 문제부터요. 보시다시피 지금은 반납에 화면 세 개를 거칩니다.)
3. Maya: "Good. Now the chart. Emphasize the main number." (좋아요. 이제 그래프요. 핵심 숫자를 힘주어 말해요.)
4. Jiwoo: "This chart shows our test data. I’d like to draw your attention to this bar. Approximately sixty percent of users couldn’t find the return button." (저희 테스트 결과 그래프입니다. 이 막대를 봐 주십시오. 사용자 약 60%가 반납 버튼을 못 찾았습니다.)
5. Maya: "Strong. Then?" (힘 있네요. 그다음은요?)
6. Jiwoo: "This brings me to my next point, our solution. You tap the big map button, check the station, and you’re done." (이제 다음 내용, 저희 해결책으로 넘어가겠습니다. 큰 지도 버튼을 누르고 대여소를 확인하면 끝입니다.)
7. Maya: "Say it like you mean it!" (진심을 담아서 말해 봐요!)
8. Jiwoo: "All on one screen! To sum up, the new screen is faster and easier. Thank you for listening." (모두 한 화면에서요! 정리하면, 새 화면은 더 빠르고 더 쉽습니다. 들어 주셔서 감사합니다.)
9. Maya: "Perfect. Oh, here they come!" (완벽해요. 아, 들어오네요!)
10. Designer: "(After the presentation) Great talk, Jiwoo. Quick question. How did you calculate that percentage?" ((발표가 끝난 뒤) 좋은 발표였어요, 지우 씨. 간단히 하나 물을게요. 그 퍼센트는 어떻게 계산했어요?)
11. Jiwoo: "Good question. We tested eight users, and five couldn’t find the button." (좋은 질문이에요. 사용자 여덟 명을 테스트했는데, 그중 다섯 명이 버튼을 찾지 못했어요.)
Go by the answers above, not by what the learner says: if their answer is the other one, say so kindly and show the line. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/아니에요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. Give the verdict in the language you are using with this learner. Only when you are speaking Korean to them, say it as 정답은 True예요 / 정답은 False예요. There are 3 statements: ask every one and wait for an answer to each (Oh or Hmm is not an answer). Only after you have checked the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

frame: Today, I’d like to talk about ___.
As you can see, ___. / To sum up, ___.
head: 주제
보여 주기 (As you can see, …)
정리 (To sum up, …)
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: Today, I’d like to talk about ___. / As you can see, ___. / To sum up, ___. Table (주제 → 보여 주기 (As you can see, …)):
- our new return screen → it takes one screen.
- the city’s bike lanes → there are more downtown.
- our team survey → most people like short meetings.
- my favorite café → it’s busiest at 8 a.m.
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
Today, I’d like to talk about … 주제 밝히기 
I’ve divided my talk into three parts. 순서 알려 주기 
Let’s start with … 첫 내용 시작 
This brings me to my next point. 다음 내용으로

As you can see, … · This chart shows … 자료 보여 주기 
To sum up, … · In conclusion, … 정리하기 
Thank you for listening. 끝인사
errors: I’d like to talk our new screen.
I’d like to talk about our new screen.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- 발표 열기 · 다음으로 넘어가기: Today, I’d like to talk about … 주제 밝히기 / I’ve divided my talk into three parts. 순서 알려 주기 / Let’s start with … 첫 내용 시작 / This brings me to my next point. 다음 내용으로
- 자료 보여 주기 · 마무리: As you can see, … · This chart shows … 자료 보여 주기 / To sum up, … · In conclusion, … 정리하기 / Thank you for listening. 끝인사
Common mistakes on screen:
- I’d like to talk our new screen. → I’d like to talk about our new screen. (‘~에 대해 말하다’는 talk about + 주제.)
- To summary, it’s faster. → To sum up, it’s faster. (summary는 명사예요. ‘정리하면’은 To sum up.)
- Thank you for your listening. → Thank you for listening. (listening 앞에 your를 쓰지 않아요.)
There are 2 grammar points and 3 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: 발표 열기 · 다음으로 넘어가기: Today, I’d like to talk about … 주제 밝히기 I’ve divided my talk into three parts. 순서 알려 주기 Let’s start with … 첫 내용 시작 This brings me to my next point. 다음 내용으로
자료 보여 주기 · 마무리: As you can see, … · This chart shows … 자료 보여 주기 To sum up, … · In conclusion, … 정리하기 Thank you for listening. 끝인사
mistakes: I’d like to talk our new screen. → I’d like to talk about our new screen.
To summary, it’s faster. → To sum up, it’s faster.
Thank you for your listening. → Thank you for listening.

steps.note: 예) our new screen / one screen → Today, I’d like to talk about our new screen. As you can see, it takes only one screen. To sum up, it’s faster.
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) our new screen / one screen → Today, I’d like to talk about our new screen. As you can see, it takes only one screen. To sum up, it’s faster. The items (the words the learner gets for each one): our new screen / one screen | our survey / short meetings | the bike lanes / more downtown | my café / busy at 8 a.m.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

cards: Today, I’d like to talk about ___.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "Today, I’d like to talk about…" (짧은 발표); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "Today, I’d like to talk about ___." / "As you can see, ___." / "To sum up, ___.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: I’ve divided my talk into three parts.
This brings me to my next point.
Let me give you an example.
I’d like to draw your attention to ___.
I’m happy to take any questions.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 발표 순서 잡기: "I’ve divided my talk into three parts." (발표를 세 부분으로 나눴습니다., 정중); "Let’s start with ___." (~부터 시작하겠습니다., 보통); "This brings me to my next point." (이제 다음 내용으로 넘어가겠습니다., 정중); "Let me give you an example." (예를 하나 들어 보겠습니다., 보통)
- 자료 보여 주기: "This chart shows ___." (이 그래프는 ~를 보여 줍니다., 보통); "I’d like to draw your attention to ___." (~에 주목해 주십시오., 정중)
- 마무리하기: "In conclusion, ___." (결론적으로 ~., 정중); "Thank you for listening." (들어 주셔서 감사합니다., 정중); "I’m happy to take any questions." (질문이 있으시면 기꺼이 받겠습니다., 정중)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 발표 낱말

an *introduction* 도입, 첫 부분 · an *outline* 발표 개요 
 the main *concept* 핵심 개념 · *analyze* 분석하다 
 *demonstrate* (직접 해 보이며) 시연하다 · *emphasize* 강조하다 
 a *pitch* (아이디어를 파는) 짧은 제안 발표 · *estimate* 어림, 추정치
(참고) shut up은 조심해요

*Shut up!* 입 다물어! 아주 무례한 말이라 직장에서는 쓰지 않아요. 
 부드럽게: Could we have a moment of quiet, please? 잠시 조용히 해 주시겠어요?
steps.blank:
A: Today, I’d like to talk ___ our new screen. I’ve divided my talk ___ three parts. 
A: As you can ___, returning a bike takes three screens. 
A: To sum ___, the new screen is faster. Thank you for ___. 
낱말 상자: about · into · see · up · listening
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 발표 낱말: an introduction 도입, 첫 부분 · an outline 발표 개요 / the main concept 핵심 개념 · analyze 분석하다 / demonstrate (직접 해 보이며) 시연하다 · emphasize 강조하다 / a pitch (아이디어를 파는) 짧은 제안 발표 · estimate 어림, 추정치
- (참고) shut up은 조심해요: Shut up! 입 다물어! 아주 무례한 말이라 직장에서는 쓰지 않아요. / 부드럽게: Could we have a moment of quiet, please? 잠시 조용히 해 주시겠어요?
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: Today, I’d like to talk ___ our new screen. I’ve divided my talk ___ three parts. / A: As you can ___, returning a bike takes three screens. / A: To sum ___, the new screen is faster. Thank you for ___. / 낱말 상자: about · into · see · up · listening
Go through every point in each tip box (for example every greeting with its time of day), one or two short sentences each, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, one blank per turn: stop at the blank, wait for them to fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: presentation (발표), slide (슬라이드(발표 화면 한 장)), chart (도표, 차트), graph (그래프), data (자료, 데이터), audience (청중, 관객), speech (연설), highlight (강조하다; 강조 표시), profit (이익, 수익), section (부분, 구역), structure (구조, 짜임), analysis (분석).
Go through about six, new ones first, one word per turn: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and wait for the learner to say it before the next word. Never give several words in one turn. After every two or three words, ask one tiny real question with the word you just did (for example: Are you a morning person?), wait for the answer and react; do this at least twice in this part. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: Today’s topic is our new screen.
Let me illustrate with an example.
These figures come from our test.
Let me introduce our new screen.
I’m happy to take any questions.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: topic (주제) — "Today’s topic is our new screen."; conclusion (결론, 맺음말) — "In conclusion, it’s faster."; attention (주의, 주목) — "Thank you for your attention."; illustrate ((예·그림으로) 설명하다) — "Let me illustrate with an example."; figure (수치, 숫자(앞에서는 ‘figure out 알아내다’)) — "These figures come from our test."; summary (요약) — "a one-slide summary"; introduce (소개하다) — "Let me introduce our new screen."; question (질문) — "I’m happy to take any questions.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: Open your talk about a place you like.
Today, I’d like to talk about ___.
Point to your (made-up) chart. What does it show?
As you can see, it’s busiest on ___.
To sum up, ___. Thank you for listening.
How do you feel before a presentation? How do you prepare?
I usually feel ___. I practice by ___ing.
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Open your talk about a place you like." (hint on screen: Today, I’d like to talk about ___.)
- "Point to your (made-up) chart. What does it show?" (hint on screen: As you can see, it’s busiest on ___.)
- "End your talk." (hint on screen: To sum up, ___. Thank you for listening.)
- "How do you feel before a presentation? How do you prepare?" (hint on screen: I usually feel ___. I practice by ___ing.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.
questions: Open your talk about a place you like.
Point to your (made-up) chart. What does it show?
End your talk.
How do you feel before a presentation? How do you prepare?

steps.title: The Real Thing
steps.text: By ten past nine, the presentation was *in full swing*. Twelve people from Vancouver occupied the screen. Jiwoo’s talk *consisted of* three parts, and every slide had one theme: pure white with an orange highlight. Her demonstration showed how the new design *brings* the number of screens *down* from three to one. “*In the light of* our test, we rebuilt the foundation of the return flow,” she said. Then the Vancouver lead spoke. “The screen *in question* could *bring about* fewer problems for riders. Let’s use it in Vancouver, too.” To Jiwoo’s delight, everyone agreed. Maya smiled. “A clear pitch. That’s what characterizes a good speaker.”
steps.gloss: in full swing 한창인 · occupy 차지하다, 채우다 · consist of ~로 이루어지다 · pure 순수한, 티 없는 · bring down 낮추다, 줄이다 · in the light of ~에 비추어, ~를 고려해 · foundation 기초, 토대 · in question 지금 말하는, 문제의 · bring about 가져오다, 일으키다 · delight 기쁨 · characterize ~의 특징이 되다
questions: What did the new design bring down?
What did the Vancouver team decide?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "The Real Thing". Text: "By ten past nine, the presentation was in full swing. Twelve people from Vancouver occupied the screen. Jiwoo’s talk consisted of three parts, and every slide had one theme: pure white with an orange highlight. Her demonstration showed how the new design brings the number of screens down from three to one. “In the light of our test, we rebuilt the foundation of the return flow,” she said. Then the Vancouver lead spoke. “The screen in question could bring about fewer problems for riders. Let’s use it in Vancouver, too.” To Jiwoo’s delight, everyone agreed. Maya smiled. “A clear pitch. That’s what characterizes a good speaker.”" Words: in full swing 한창인 · occupy 차지하다, 채우다 · consist of ~로 이루어지다 · pure 순수한, 티 없는 · bring down 낮추다, 줄이다 · in the light of ~에 비추어, ~를 고려해 · foundation 기초, 토대 · in question 지금 말하는, 문제의 · bring about 가져오다, 일으키다 · delight 기쁨 · characterize ~의 특징이 되다.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "What did the new design bring down?" / "What did the Vancouver team decide?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘Today, I’d like to talk about ___.’로 발표를 시작하며 주제를 밝힐 수 있어요.
‘As you can see, ___.’로 자료를 가리키며 설명할 수 있어요.
‘To sum up, ___.’로 발표 내용을 정리하며 마무리할 수 있어요.
steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘Today, I’d like to talk about ___.’로 발표를 시작하며 주제를 밝힐 수 있어요.
- ‘As you can see, ___.’로 자료를 가리키며 설명할 수 있어요.
- ‘To sum up, ___.’로 발표 내용을 정리하며 마무리할 수 있어요.
First ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence, and stop there to wait. React and praise specifically. Only then, in a later turn, end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to it, say that the next lesson is waiting for next time, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

lessons.title: 그랬음에 틀림없어요
lessons.title_en: It must have gone to the wrong floor.
lessons.goal: 지난 일을 근거로 추측하기

steps.title: 그랬음에 틀림없어요
steps.title_en: It must have gone to the wrong floor.
steps.goal: 지난 일을 근거로 추측하기
steps.scene_desc: 2월 초 토요일 오후, 아파트 3층 복도. 휴대폰을 들고 당황한 표정의 지우와, 턱에 손을 대고 탐정처럼 생각하는 벤. 복도 끝 회색 문 옆 작은 화분 곁에 굵은 테이프를 두른 긴 상자가 놓여 있음(화면·문·벽에 글자와 숫자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "It must have gone to the wrong floor." (그랬음에 틀림없어요). Goal: 지난 일을 근거로 추측하기. Today's scene: 2월 초 토요일 오후, 아파트 3층 복도. 휴대폰을 들고 당황한 표정의 지우와, 턱에 손을 대고 탐정처럼 생각하는 벤. 복도 끝 회색 문 옆 작은 화분 곁에 굵은 테이프를 두른 긴 상자가 놓여 있음. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Ben, Jiwoo.
