There are 3 statements: ask every one and wait for an answer to each (Oh or Hmm is not an answer). Only after you have checked the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

frame: He can’t have ___. / Maybe they just forgot.
head: 있었던 일
내 추측 (must / might / can’t have)
그렇게 생각하는 이유
rows: She must have left it on the wrong floor.
He might have missed the email.
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: She must have ___. / He can’t have ___. / Maybe they just forgot. Table (있었던 일 → 내 추측 (must / might / can’t have)):
- The box isn’t here. → She must have left it on the wrong floor.
- He didn’t reply. → He might have missed the email.
- The cake is gone. → Someone must have eaten it.
- My umbrella is gone. → She can’t have taken it.
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
She *must have left* it. (거의 확실) 
They *might have missed* it. (어쩌면) 
He *can’t* (= *couldn’t*) *have taken* it. (그럴 리 없음)
지금·과거 must be · must have been

There *must be* a reason. (지금) 
You *must have been* worried. (과거) 
과거분사: take → taken, eat → eaten
errors: She must left it on the wrong floor.
She must have left it on the wrong floor.
You must have been worried yesterday.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- must / might / can’t have + 과거분사: She must have left it. (거의 확실) / They might have missed it. (어쩌면) / He can’t (= couldn’t) have taken it. (그럴 리 없음)
- 지금·과거 must be · must have been: There must be a reason. (지금) / You must have been worried. (과거) / 과거분사: take → taken, eat → eaten
Common mistakes on screen:
- She must left it on the wrong floor. → She must have left it on the wrong floor. (must 뒤에 have를 넣어요.)
- He can’t have take it. → He can’t have taken it. (have 뒤에는 과거분사 taken.)
- You must be worried yesterday. → You must have been worried yesterday. (과거는 must have been.)
There are 2 grammar points and 3 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: must / might / can’t have + 과거분사: She must have left it. (거의 확실) They might have missed it. (어쩌면) He can’t (= couldn’t) have taken it. (그럴 리 없음)
지금·과거 must be · must have been: There must be a reason. (지금) You must have been worried. (과거) 과거분사: take → taken, eat → eaten
mistakes: She must left it on the wrong floor. → She must have left it on the wrong floor.
He can’t have take it. → He can’t have taken it.
You must be worried yesterday. → You must have been worried yesterday.

steps.note: 예) → She must have missed the bus. · have 뒤에 과거분사를 써요.
items: She was in Busan all day.
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) → She must have missed the bus. · have 뒤에 과거분사를 써요. The items (the words the learner gets for each one): My friend is late. / must have · miss the bus | The cake is gone. / someone must have · eat it | He didn’t reply. / might have · miss the email | She was in Busan all day. / can’t have · take my umbrella.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "It must have gone to the wrong floor." (그랬음에 틀림없어요); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "She must have ___." / "He can’t have ___." / "Maybe they just forgot.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: They might have missed the email.
It must have been a mistake.
그 사람은 알 수가 없었을 거예요.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 지난 일 추측하기: "They might have missed the email." (이메일을 못 봤을지도 몰라요., 보통); "He must have been tired." (분명 피곤했을 거예요., 보통); "It must have been a mistake." (실수였던 게 분명해요., 보통); "Someone must have taken it." (누가 가져간 게 틀림없어요., 보통)
- 그럴 리 없음 · 이유 찾기: "She couldn’t have known." (그 사람은 알 수가 없었을 거예요., 보통); "There must be a reason." (분명 이유가 있을 거예요., 보통); "That would explain it." (그래서 그랬구나. 그러면 설명이 되네요., 친근)
- 수수께끼 마무리: "You must have been worried." (걱정 많이 했겠어요., 친근); "I guess we’ll never know." (영영 모르겠네요., 친근)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 범죄 드라마 낱말 (참고)

a *criminal* 범죄자 · a *victim* 피해자 · a *witness* 목격자 
The police *investigate* and *arrest* someone. 경찰이 수사하고 체포해요. 
A *judge* decides in court. 판사가 법정에서 판결해요. · *legal* 법의, 법률상의 
드라마·뉴스에 자주 나와요. 오늘 이야기는 그냥 잃어버린 상자예요!
이야기 속 작은 낱말

*beside* the door 문 옆에 · a *thick strip* of tape 굵은 테이프 한 줄 · a *tube* of glue 접착제 한 통 
My desk is *in disorder*. 책상이 엉망이에요. · *encounter* 우연히 만나다 · a kind *gentleman* 친절한 신사분 
(참고) Oh my god은 피하는 사람도 있어요. Oh my gosh가 더 부드러워요.
steps.blank:
A: The app says “delivered,” but my box isn’t here. Someone must have ___ it!   B: Let’s step ___ for a second. 
A: The driver might ___ left it on the wrong floor.   B: Or maybe they just ___ to bring it. 
낱말 상자: taken · back · have · forgot
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 범죄 드라마 낱말 (참고): a criminal 범죄자 · a victim 피해자 · a witness 목격자 / The police investigate and arrest someone. 경찰이 수사하고 체포해요. / A judge decides in court. 판사가 법정에서 판결해요. · legal 법의, 법률상의 / 드라마·뉴스에 자주 나와요. 오늘 이야기는 그냥 잃어버린 상자예요!
- 이야기 속 작은 낱말: beside the door 문 옆에 · a thick strip of tape 굵은 테이프 한 줄 · a tube of glue 접착제 한 통 / My desk is in disorder. 책상이 엉망이에요. · encounter 우연히 만나다 · a kind gentleman 친절한 신사분 / (참고) Oh my god은 피하는 사람도 있어요. Oh my gosh가 더 부드러워요.
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: The app says “delivered,” but my box isn’t here. Someone must have ___ it! B: Let’s step ___ for a second. / A: The driver might ___ left it on the wrong floor. B: Or maybe they just ___ to bring it. / 낱말 상자: taken · back · have · forgot
Go through every point in each tip box (for example every greeting with its time of day), one or two short sentences each, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, one blank per turn: stop at the blank, wait for them to fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: judge (판사), witness (목격자), arrest (체포하다), criminal (범죄자), victim (피해자), detect (알아차리다, 찾아내다), proof (증명, 증거), accident (사고), investigate (조사하다, 수사하다), legal (법의, 법률상의). Review words: clue (단서), evidence (증거).
Go through about six, new ones first, one word per turn: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and wait for the learner to say it before the next word. Never give several words in one turn. After every two or three words, ask one tiny real question with the word you just did (for example: Are you a morning person?), wait for the answer and react; do this at least twice in this part. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: I concluded it was a mistake.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: conclude (결론을 내리다) — "I concluded it was a mistake."; obviously (분명히, 누가 봐도) — "Obviously, nobody took it."; logical (논리적인, 앞뒤가 맞는) — "a logical guess"; theory (가설, (어떤 일을 설명하는) 생각) — "Ben had two theories."; investigation (조사, 수사) — "a police investigation"; assume ((증거 없이) 그렇다고 여기다) — "I assumed someone took it."; cause (원인) — "the cause of the problem"; reason (이유) — "There must be a reason."; mistake (실수) — "It was a mistake."; probably (아마) — "It’s probably downstairs.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: Your friend is 30 minutes late. Make a guess.
She must have ___. / She might have ___.
Your package says “delivered,” but it isn’t there. What do you say?
It must have gone to the wrong door.
A coworker missed a meeting. Make a kind guess.
He might have missed the email.
Do you like detective stories? Why?
Yes. I love guessing ___. / Not really.
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Your friend is 30 minutes late. Make a guess." (hint on screen: She must have ___. / She might have ___.)
- "Your package says “delivered,” but it isn’t there. What do you say?" (hint on screen: It must have gone to the wrong door.)
- "A coworker missed a meeting. Make a kind guess." (hint on screen: He might have missed the email.)
- "Do you like detective stories? Why?" (hint on screen: Yes. I love guessing ___. / Not really.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.
questions: Your friend is 30 minutes late. Make a guess.
Your package says “delivered,” but it isn’t there. What do you say?
A coworker missed a meeting. Make a kind guess.
Do you like detective stories? Why?

steps.title: Case Closed
steps.text: That evening, Jiwoo put the lamp beside her laptop, but first she cleaned her desk. It was in total disorder! Then she told Grace the story. “Ben had two logical theories: the wrong floor, or a company that forgot. *The former* was right, and the missing number *accounts for* it.” Grace laughed. “Ben is *known to* love detective shows. He’s *a bit of a* detective himself.” The next morning, Jiwoo encountered the building manager, a kind gentleman, in the elevator. He had a tube of glue and a new number sign. “No more accidents,” he said. Jiwoo concluded that *nothing but* a tiny sign had caused all the trouble. No criminal, no victim, just a bright lamp.
steps.gloss: in disorder 엉망인, 어질러진 · theory 가설, 추측 · the former (둘 중) 앞의 것, 전자 · account for 설명하다, ~의 이유가 되다 · known to ~하는 것으로 알려진 · a bit of a 약간 ~ 같은 사람 · encounter 우연히 만나다 · nothing but 오직 ~뿐
questions: Which of Ben’s theories was right?
What did the building manager have?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "Case Closed". Text: "That evening, Jiwoo put the lamp beside her laptop, but first she cleaned her desk. It was in total disorder! Then she told Grace the story. “Ben had two logical theories: the wrong floor, or a company that forgot. The former was right, and the missing number accounts for it.” Grace laughed. “Ben is known to love detective shows. He’s a bit of a detective himself.” The next morning, Jiwoo encountered the building manager, a kind gentleman, in the elevator. He had a tube of glue and a new number sign. “No more accidents,” he said. Jiwoo concluded that nothing but a tiny sign had caused all the trouble. No criminal, no victim, just a bright lamp." Words: in disorder 엉망인, 어질러진 · theory 가설, 추측 · the former (둘 중) 앞의 것, 전자 · account for 설명하다, ~의 이유가 되다 · known to ~하는 것으로 알려진 · a bit of a 약간 ~ 같은 사람 · encounter 우연히 만나다 · nothing but 오직 ~뿐.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "Which of Ben’s theories was right?" / "What did the building manager have?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘She must have ___.’로 지난 일을 강하게 추측할 수 있어요.
‘He can’t have ___.’로 지난 일이 그럴 리 없다고 말할 수 있어요.
‘Maybe they just forgot.’으로 부드럽고 너그럽게 추측할 수 있어요.
steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘She must have ___.’로 지난 일을 강하게 추측할 수 있어요.
- ‘He can’t have ___.’로 지난 일이 그럴 리 없다고 말할 수 있어요.
- ‘Maybe they just forgot.’으로 부드럽고 너그럽게 추측할 수 있어요.
First ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence, and stop there to wait. React and praise specifically. Only then, in a later turn, end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to it, say that the next lesson is waiting for next time, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

lessons.title: 불만 말하기
lessons.goal: 서비스에 불만을 분명하게 말하고 해결을 요구하기

steps.title: 불만 말하기
steps.goal: 서비스에 불만을 분명하게 말하고 해결을 요구하기
steps.scene_desc: 2월 중순 저녁, 그레이스네 거실. 탁자 위에 받침이 플라스틱인 책상 램프가 깜빡이고, 지우가 휴대폰을 귀에 대고 차분하지만 단호한 표정으로 통화하며, 옆에서 그레이스가 엄지를 들어 응원함(화면·상자에 글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "This isn’t what I expected." (불만 말하기). Goal: 서비스에 불만을 분명하게 말하고 해결을 요구하기. Today's scene: 2월 중순 저녁, 그레이스네 거실. 탁자 위에 받침이 플라스틱인 책상 램프가 깜빡이고, 지우가 휴대폰을 귀에 대고 차분하지만 단호한 표정으로 통화하며, 옆에서 그레이스가 엄지를 들어 응원함. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Grace, Jiwoo, Agent. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "I’m not happy with ___.".

steps.when: 불만을 차분하게 꺼내요. 그다음 바로 문제를 말해요.
steps.extra: I’m not happy with this lamp. The light keeps flickering.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "I’m not happy with ___." (~가 마음에 안 들어요. ~에 불만이 있어요.). When to use it: 불만을 차분하게 꺼내요. 그다음 바로 문제를 말해요. Note: I’m not happy with this lamp. The light keeps flickering.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "This isn’t what I expected.".

steps.when: 물건이나 서비스가 생각과 다를 때 말해요. *what* = ~하는 것.
steps.extra: This isn’t what I ordered. · This isn’t what I was promised.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "This isn’t what I expected." (기대했던 것과 달라요.). When to use it: 물건이나 서비스가 생각과 다를 때 말해요. what = ~하는 것. Note: This isn’t what I ordered. · This isn’t what I was promised.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) Give a different everyday moment where they need it, and let them say it there.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "I’d like to speak to the manager.".

steps.en: I’d like to speak to the manager.
steps.when: 공손하지만 단호한 말이에요. 처음 응대한 사람이 해결해 주지 못할 때 써요.
steps.extra: I understand it’s not your fault. But I’d like to speak to the manager.
steps.teach:

Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) Give a different everyday moment where they need it, and let them say it there.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.

steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: I’m not happy with ___. / This isn’t what I expected. / I’d like to speak to the manager. Table (문제 → 다르다고 말하기 (This isn’t what …)):
- The color is wrong. → This isn’t what I ordered.
- The lamp is faulty. → This isn’t what I expected.
- The room is noisy. → This isn’t what I was promised.
- The soup is cold. → This isn’t what I asked for.
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
This isn’t *what* I ordered. 주문한 게 아니에요. 
This isn’t *what* I expected. 기대와 달라요. 
This is exactly *what* I wanted! 딱 원하던 거예요!

문제: I’m not happy *with* the lamp. 
원하는 해결: I’d like a new one. · 약속받은 내용: I *was promised* a steel base. 
부드럽게: I understand it’s not your fault.

I’d like to speak to the manager.
I was promise a new lamp.
I was promised a new lamp.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- This isn’t what ~ (what = ~하는 것): This isn’t what I ordered. 주문한 게 아니에요. / This isn’t what I expected. 기대와 달라요. / This is exactly what I wanted! 딱 원하던 거예요!
- 분명하게, 그러면서 공손하게: 문제: I’m not happy with the lamp. / 원하는 해결: I’d like a new one. · 약속받은 내용: I was promised a steel base. / 부드럽게: I understand it’s not your fault.
Common mistakes on screen:
- This isn’t that I expected. → This isn’t what I expected. (‘~하는 것’은 what.)
- I’d like to speak the manager. → I’d like to speak to the manager. (speak 뒤에 to를 넣어요.)
- I was promise a new lamp. → I was promised a new lamp. (‘약속받았다’는 was promised.)
There are 2 grammar points and 3 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) → I’m not happy with the lamp. It’s faulty. I’d like a full refund. The items (the words the learner gets for each one): the lamp · faulty / a full refund | the jacket · wrong color / an exchange | the room · noisy / a different room | the delivery · late again / to speak to the manager.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

cards: I’d like to speak to the manager.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "This isn’t what I expected." (불만 말하기); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "I’m not happy with ___." / "This isn’t what I expected." / "I’d like to speak to the manager.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: I’d like to make a complaint.
This is the second time this has happened.
What are you going to do about it?
I understand it’s not your fault.
I hope it won’t happen again.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 불만 말하기: "I’d like to make a complaint." (불만 사항을 말씀드리고 싶어요., 정중); "This is the second time this has happened." (이런 일이 벌써 두 번째예요., 보통); "I was promised ___." (~를 해 준다고 약속받았어요., 보통); "That’s not acceptable." (그건 받아들일 수 없어요., 보통)
- 조치 요구하기: "I expect a full refund." (전액 환불해 주셔야 해요., 보통); "What are you going to do about it?" (어떻게 해결해 주실 건가요?, 보통)
- 공손함 지키기: "I understand it’s not your fault." (그쪽 잘못이 아닌 건 알아요., 정중); "I appreciate your help." (도와주셔서 감사해요., 정중); "I hope it won’t happen again." (다시는 이런 일이 없으면 좋겠어요., 정중)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 전화하기 전에 (참고)

문제를 먼저, 원하는 것을 그다음에 말해요. 차분하게요. 
Don’t fall into the *trap* of shouting. 소리부터 지르는 함정에 빠지지 마세요. 
이야기 속 가게는 지어낸 곳이에요. 환불·교환 규정은 가게마다 다르니 판매처 규정을 확인하세요.
이야기 속 낱말

a *steel* base 강철(스틸) 받침 · the *inner* wire 안쪽 전선 
a sticky *substance* 끈적한 물질 · a *vice president* 부사장
steps.blank:
A: I’m not happy ___ this lamp. This isn’t ___ I ordered.   B: I’m sorry. I can offer you a ___. 
A: I understand it’s not your fault, but I’d like to speak ___ the manager. 
낱말 상자: with · what · voucher · to
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 전화하기 전에 (참고): 문제를 먼저, 원하는 것을 그다음에 말해요. 차분하게요. / Don’t fall into the trap of shouting. 소리부터 지르는 함정에 빠지지 마세요. / 이야기 속 가게는 지어낸 곳이에요. 환불·교환 규정은 가게마다 다르니 판매처 규정을 확인하세요.
- 이야기 속 낱말: a steel base 강철(스틸) 받침 · the inner wire 안쪽 전선 / a sticky substance 끈적한 물질 · a vice president 부사장
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: I’m not happy ___ this lamp. This isn’t ___ I ordered. B: I’m sorry. I can offer you a ___. / A: I understand it’s not your fault, but I’d like to speak ___ the manager. / 낱말 상자: with · what · voucher · to
Go through every point in each tip box (for example every greeting with its time of day), one or two short sentences each, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, one blank per turn: stop at the blank, wait for them to fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: voucher (상품권, 할인권), refund (환불), faulty (결함이 있는), defective ((처음부터) 불량인), compensation (보상), escalate ((윗사람에게) 올리다), complaint (불만, 항의), manager (책임자, 관리자), service (서비스, 응대), quality (품질), promise (약속하다). Review words: policy (규정, 정책).
Go through about six, new ones first, one word per turn: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and wait for the learner to say it before the next word. Never give several words in one turn. After every two or three words, ask one tiny real question with the word you just did (for example: Are you a morning person?), wait for the answer and react; do this at least twice in this part. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: It was resolved in a day.
I don’t like to complain, but…
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: expectation (기대) — "It didn’t meet my expectations."; acceptable (받아들일 만한, 괜찮은) — "That’s not acceptable."; unacceptable (받아들일 수 없는) — "The delay is unacceptable."; standard (기준, 수준) — "below our standard"; resolve (해결하다) — "It was resolved in a day."; assure (장담하다, 확실히 말하다) — "I assure you she’ll call."; complain (불평하다, 항의하다) — "I don’t like to complain, but…"; expect (기대하다, 예상하다) — "I expect a full refund."; responsible ((~을) 맡은, 책임지는) — "She’s responsible for service.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: Call the store about something you bought that had a problem.
I’d like to make a complaint. My ___ is faulty.
The agent offers a voucher, but you want a new one. What do you say?
Thanks, but I’d like a new one, please.
How do you stay polite when you complain?
I say, “I understand it’s not your fault.”
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Call the store about something you bought that had a problem." (hint on screen: I’d like to make a complaint. My ___ is faulty.)
- "The agent offers a voucher, but you want a new one. What do you say?" (hint on screen: Thanks, but I’d like a new one, please.)
- "How do you stay polite when you complain?" (hint on screen: I say, “I understand it’s not your fault.”)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.
questions: Call the store about something you bought that had a problem.
The agent offers a voucher, but you want a new one. What do you say?
How do you stay polite when you complain?

steps.title: A Call Back
steps.text: Later that evening, the manager called. “I’m very concerned about what happened,” she said. “*With regard to* your lamp, the inner wire was defective. That’s below our standard.” She refunded Jiwoo *in full* *on the grounds* that the lamp didn’t match the description, and she added a voucher as compensation. “I appreciate your help,” said Jiwoo. Later, Jiwoo *made her way* to Grace’s door. “It was resolved in one day!” “Calm, clear complaints always *stand out*,” said Grace. “*But then again*, you’re good at this.” Jiwoo laughed. “Maybe I should be vice president of complaints!”
steps.gloss: concerned about ~를 걱정하는 · (참고) be concerned with ~에 관한 것이다: Our policy is concerned with returns. · with regard to ~에 관해 · in full 전부, 전액 · on the grounds that ~라는 이유로 · make one’s way 가다, 향하다 · stand out 눈에 띄다 · but then again 하지만 한편으로는
questions: Why did Jiwoo get a full refund?
What did the manager offer as compensation?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "A Call Back". Text: "Later that evening, the manager called. “I’m very concerned about what happened,” she said. “With regard to your lamp, the inner wire was defective. That’s below our standard.” She refunded Jiwoo in full on the grounds that the lamp didn’t match the description, and she added a voucher as compensation. “I appreciate your help,” said Jiwoo. Later, Jiwoo made her way to Grace’s door. “It was resolved in one day!” “Calm, clear complaints always stand out,” said Grace. “But then again, you’re good at this.” Jiwoo laughed. “Maybe I should be vice president of complaints!”" Words: concerned about ~를 걱정하는 · (참고) be concerned with ~에 관한 것이다: Our policy is concerned with returns. · with regard to ~에 관해 · in full 전부, 전액 · on the grounds that ~라는 이유로 · make one’s way 가다, 향하다 · stand out 눈에 띄다 · but then again 하지만 한편으로는.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "Why did Jiwoo get a full refund?" / "What did the manager offer as compensation?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘I’m not happy with ___.’로 차분하게 불만을 꺼낼 수 있어요.
‘This isn’t what I expected.’로 기대와 다르다고 말할 수 있어요.
‘I’d like to speak to the manager.’로 책임자와 이야기하고 싶다고 공손하게 요청할 수 있어요.
steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘I’m not happy with ___.’로 차분하게 불만을 꺼낼 수 있어요.
- ‘This isn’t what I expected.’로 기대와 다르다고 말할 수 있어요.
- ‘I’d like to speak to the manager.’로 책임자와 이야기하고 싶다고 공손하게 요청할 수 있어요.
First ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence, and stop there to wait. React and praise specifically. Only then, in a later turn, end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to it, say that the next lesson is waiting for next time, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

lessons.title: 일과 삶의 균형

steps.title: 일과 삶의 균형
steps.goal: 일이 많다고 말하고 쉬는 계획과 균형을 이야기하기
steps.scene_desc: 2월 하순 금요일 저녁, 회사 근처 아늑한 식당. 지친 표정의 지우가 턱을 괴고 앉아 있고, 맞은편 클로이가 손을 펼치며 드라마 주인공 흉내를 내듯 장난스럽게 말함. 탁자 위 찌개 냄비와 밥공기 두 개(간판·메뉴판에 글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "I’m swamped with work." (일과 삶의 균형). Goal: 일이 많다고 말하고 쉬는 계획과 균형을 이야기하기. Today's scene: 2월 하순 금요일 저녁, 회사 근처 아늑한 식당. 지친 표정의 지우가 턱을 괴고 앉아 있고, 맞은편 클로이가 손을 펼치며 드라마 주인공 흉내를 내듯 장난스럽게 말함. 탁자 위 찌개 냄비와 밥공기 두 개. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Chloe, Jiwoo. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "I’m swamped with ___.".

steps.when: 아주 바쁘다고 말해요. *with + 명사*.
steps.extra: I’m swamped with work. · I’m swamped with emails.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "I’m swamped with ___." (~에 파묻혀 있어요. ~ 때문에 정신없이 바빠요.). When to use it: 아주 바쁘다고 말해요. with + 명사. Note: I’m swamped with work. · I’m swamped with emails.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "I need to take some time off.".

steps.en: I need to take some time off.
steps.when: 일이나 학교를 잠시 쉬어야 할 때 말해요.
steps.extra: I need to take some time off. Maybe three days in March.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "I need to take some time off." (좀 쉬어야겠어요. 휴가를 좀 내야겠어요.). When to use it: 일이나 학교를 잠시 쉬어야 할 때 말해요. Note: I need to take some time off. Maybe three days in March.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) Give a different everyday moment where they need it, and let them say it there.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "I try to keep work and life separate.".

steps.en: I try to keep work and life separate.
steps.when: 균형을 어떻게 지키는지 말해요. keep + 대상 + *형용사*.
steps.extra: I try to keep work and life separate. I don’t check emails after work.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "I try to keep work and life separate." (일과 생활을 나누려고 해요.). When to use it: 균형을 어떻게 지키는지 말해요. keep + 대상 + 형용사. Note: I try to keep work and life separate. I don’t check emails after work.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) Give a different everyday moment where they need it, and let them say it there.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("Swamped · 2월 하순 금요일 저녁, 식당에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: Swamped · 2월 하순 금요일 저녁, 식당에서

lines.en: Jiwoo, over here! You look exhausted. Long week?
lines.ko: 지우 씨, 여기예요! 엄청 지쳐 보여요. 힘든 한 주였어요?

lines.en: The longest. Since the presentation, I’ve been swamped with work. The Vancouver team wants the new return screen by April.
lines.ko: 제일 길었어요. 발표 이후로 일에 파묻혀 지내요. 밴쿠버 팀이 새 반납 화면을 4월까지 원하거든요.

lines.en: Wow, that’s great news. But have you been working overtime?
lines.ko: 와, 좋은 소식이네요. 그런데 계속 야근하고 있는 거예요?

lines.en: Every night this week. Even at home, I can’t switch off.
lines.ko: 이번 주 내내 밤마다요. 집에서도 일 생각이 꺼지지가 않아요.

lines.en: You sound like the hero of a work drama. “Just one more email, then I’ll sleep!”
lines.ko: 직장 드라마 주인공 같아요. “메일 하나만 더 보내고 잘게!”

lines.en: Ha! That’s me. When did I last take a break? I don’t even remember.
lines.ko: 하하! 딱 저예요. 마지막으로 쉰 게 언제였는지 기억도 안 나요.

lines.en: That’s a lot of pressure, Jiwoo. Don’t work too hard.
lines.ko: 부담이 정말 크겠어요, 지우 씨. 너무 무리하지 마요.

lines.en: You’re right. {{I need to take some time off.}} Maybe three days in March?
lines.ko: 맞아요. 휴가를 좀 내야겠어요. 3월에 사흘쯤?

lines.en: Perfect. Ask Maya on Monday. You’ve earned it.
lines.ko: 좋아요. 월요일에 마야한테 말해 봐요. 그럴 자격 충분해요.

lines.en: I will. But how do you stay so relaxed?
lines.ko: 그럴게요. 그런데 클로이 씨는 어떻게 그렇게 여유로워요?

lines.en: {{I try to keep work and life separate.}} I don’t check emails after work, and my weekends are for drawing.
lines.ko: 일과 생활을 나누려고 해요. 퇴근 후에는 메일을 확인하지 않고, 주말은 그림 그리는 시간이에요.

lines.en: Separate. I like that. Starting tonight, no laptop!
lines.ko: 나눈다라, 좋네요. 오늘 밤부터 노트북 금지!

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "Swamped · 2월 하순 금요일 저녁, 식당에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:

3. Chloe: "Wow, that’s great news. But have you been working overtime?" (와, 좋은 소식이네요. 그런데 계속 야근하고 있는 거예요?)
4. Jiwoo: "Every night this week. Even at home, I can’t switch off." (이번 주 내내 밤마다요. 집에서도 일 생각이 꺼지지가 않아요.)

frame: I need to take some time off. / I try to keep work and life separate.
head: 바쁜 일 (I’m swamped with …)
쉬기
균형 지키는 법
rows: I don’t check emails after work.
I take a real lunch break.
I need to take some time off.
I try to keep work and life separate.
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: I’m swamped with ___. / I need to take some time off. / I try to keep work and life separate. Table (바쁜 일 (I’m swamped with …) → 쉬기):
- emails. → I need a day off.
- meetings. → I’m taking Friday off.
- deadlines. → I need to take some time off.
- housework. → I need a break.
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
I’m *swamped with* work. 일이 산더미예요. 
She’s *swamped with* emails. · We’re *swamped with* orders. 
of가 아니라 with: swamped with work

I need to *take some time off*. 좀 쉬어야겠어요. · I’m *taking* three days *off*. 사흘 쉬어요. 
I *took* Friday *off*. 금요일에 쉬었어요. 
*keep* work and life *separate* 일과 생활을 나눠 두다(keep + 대상 + 형용사)
errors: I keep work and life separately.
I keep work and life separate.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- be swamped with + 명사: I’m swamped with work. 일이 산더미예요. / She’s swamped with emails. · We’re swamped with orders. / of가 아니라 with: swamped with work
- take time off · keep ~ separate: I need to take some time off. 좀 쉬어야겠어요. · I’m taking three days off. 사흘 쉬어요. / I took Friday off. 금요일에 쉬었어요. / keep work and life separate 일과 생활을 나눠 두다(keep + 대상 + 형용사)
Common mistakes on screen:
- I’m swamped of work. → I’m swamped with work. (swamped 뒤에는 with.)
- I keep work and life separately. → I keep work and life separate. (keep + 대상 뒤에는 형용사(separate).)
- I’m completely burn out. → I’m completely burned out. (‘완전히 지쳤다’는 burned out(burnt도 돼요).)
There are 2 grammar points and 3 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: be swamped with + 명사: I’m swamped with work. 일이 산더미예요. She’s swamped with emails. · We’re swamped with orders. of가 아니라 with: swamped with work
take time off · keep ~ separate: I need to take some time off. 좀 쉬어야겠어요. · I’m taking three days off. 사흘 쉬어요. I took Friday off. 금요일에 쉬었어요. keep work and life separate 일과 생활을 나눠 두다(keep + 대상 + 형용사)
mistakes: I’m swamped of work. → I’m swamped with work.
I keep work and life separately. → I keep work and life separate.
I’m completely burn out. → I’m completely burned out.

steps.note: 예) emails / a day → I’m swamped with emails. I need to take a day off.
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) emails / a day → I’m swamped with emails. I need to take a day off. The items (the words the learner gets for each one): emails / a day | meetings / Friday | deadlines / a week | moving house / two days.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

cards: I need to take some time off.
I try to keep work and life separate.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "I’m swamped with work." (일과 삶의 균형); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "I’m swamped with ___." / "I need to take some time off." / "I try to keep work and life separate.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: I’ve been working overtime a lot.
I don’t check emails after work.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 너무 바쁠 때: "I’ve been working overtime a lot." (요즘 야근을 많이 하고 있어요., 보통); "I’m completely burned out." (완전히 지쳐 버렸어요. 번아웃이 왔어요., 친근); "I can’t switch off." (일 생각을 끌 수가 없어요., 친근); "I need a break." (좀 쉬어야겠어요., 친근)
- 균형 지키기: "I don’t check emails after work." (퇴근 후에는 메일을 안 봐요., 보통); "Weekends are for family." (주말은 가족과 보내요., 보통)
- 챙겨 주는 말: "Take care of yourself." (몸 잘 챙겨요., 친근); "Don’t work too hard." (너무 무리하지 마요., 친근); "You’ve earned it." (그럴 자격 있어요., 친근)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

*paid leave* 유급 휴가 · a *sabbatical* 안식 휴가(보통 몇 달)

이런 규칙을 둔 팀이 많아요.

steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 쉬는 날 이야기: paid leave 유급 휴가 · a sabbatical 안식 휴가(보통 몇 달) / occasionally 가끔, 이따금 · devote time to … ~에 시간을 쏟다 / in favour = in favor (캐나다·영국식 철자)
- 직장에서의 존중 (참고): 이런 규칙을 둔 팀이 많아요. / “Respect policy: no comments about anyone’s age, gender, religion, or whether they are gay or straight.” / 존중 규칙: 누구에 대해서든 나이·성별·종교, 동성애자인지 이성애자인지를 두고 말하지 않기. / 이야기 속 팀의 웰빙 프로그램은 지어낸 거예요.
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: You look tired. B: I am. I’m swamped ___ work. / A: You need to take some time ___. B: You’re right. I’ll try to keep work and life ___. / 낱말 상자: with · off · separate
Go through every point in each tip box (for example every greeting with its time of day), one or two short sentences each, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, one blank per turn: stop at the blank, wait for them to fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: overtime (초과 근무, 야근), burnout (번아웃(일로 완전히 지침)), workload (업무량), recharge ((에너지를) 재충전하다), boundary (경계, 선), unwind ((긴장을) 풀다, 쉬다), retreat (조용히 쉬는 곳, 휴양지), meditation (명상), vacation (휴가), hobby (취미), rest (쉬다; 휴식), break ((잠깐의) 휴식).
Go through about six, new ones first, one word per turn: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and wait for the learner to say it before the next word. Never give several words in one turn. After every two or three words, ask one tiny real question with the word you just did (for example: Are you a morning person?), wait for the answer and react; do this at least twice in this part. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

What do you do to unwind?

My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "When were you last swamped with something? (work, study, or housework)" (hint on screen: I was swamped with ___ last ___.)
- "What do you do to unwind?" (hint on screen: I usually ___. It helps me recharge.)
- "If you had three days off, what would you do?" (hint on screen: I’d ___.)
- "How do you keep work (or study) and life separate?" (hint on screen: I try not to ___ after ___.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.

steps.title: Three Days in March
steps.text: On Monday, Jiwoo asked Maya for three days of paid leave in March. “You’ve been under pressure *for some time*,” Maya said. “Our new wellbeing program is *aimed at* exactly this: rest and clear boundaries.” She *broke up* Jiwoo’s workload and shared some tasks with the team. “*In the face of* big deadlines, rest is a priority, too.” Jiwoo thought about how to recharge. Not a long sabbatical or a fancy retreat, just three quiet days to unwind, and occasionally a little meditation. She texted Chloe, “Three days off!” Chloe replied, “I’m all *in favour*! So that’s how it *played out*. Devote them to sleep!” A big smile *broke out* on Jiwoo’s face.
steps.gloss: for some time 꽤 오랫동안 · aimed at ~를 위한, ~를 목표로 한 · break up 나누다 · in the face of ~에 맞닥뜨려, ~ 앞에서 · recharge 재충전하다 · in favour 찬성하는 · play out (일이) 펼쳐지다, 결국 ~되다 · break out 갑자기 생기다, (웃음이) 번지다
questions: How did Maya help with Jiwoo’s workload?
What does Chloe tell Jiwoo to do on her days off?

steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "I ended up teaching English." (내 경력). Goal: 일을 하며 즐기는 점, 지금까지 온 길, 앞으로 하고 싶은 일 말하기. Today's scene: 2월 마지막 주말 오후, 그레이스네 거실. 창가 소파에 앉은 그레이스와 지우가 찻잔을 들고 웃으며 이야기하고, 탁자 위에 오래된 사진첩이 펼쳐져 있음(사진 속 정장 차림의 젊은 그레이스). 지우의 휴대폰이 탁자 위에서 진동함. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Jiwoo, Grace. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "What I enjoy most about my job is ___.".

steps.en: What I enjoy most about my job is ___.
steps.when: 일에서 가장 좋은 점을 말해요. is 뒤에는 명사나 *-ing*.

steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "What I enjoy most about my job is ___." (제 일에서 가장 좋은 건 ~예요.). When to use it: 일에서 가장 좋은 점을 말해요. is 뒤에는 명사나 -ing. Note: What I enjoy most about my job is helping people.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "I ended up ___ing.".

steps.title: Career Paths · 2월 마지막 주말, 그레이스네 집에서

lines.en: Grace, can I ask you something? Did you always want to be a teacher?
lines.ko: 그레이스, 뭐 하나 물어봐도 돼요? 원래부터 선생님이 되고 싶었어요?

lines.en: Not at all! I started out as a consultant in the travel industry.
lines.ko: 전혀요! 처음엔 여행 업계에서 컨설턴트로 일했어요.

lines.en: Really? So how did you get into teaching?
lines.ko: 정말요? 그럼 어떻게 가르치는 일을 하게 됐어요?

lines.en: I resigned and came to Seoul for one year, just for fun. I taught a few classes, and {{I ended up}} staying and teaching English!
lines.ko: 일을 그만두고 재미 삼아 1년만 서울에 왔어요. 몇 번 가르치다가 결국 눌러앉아 영어를 가르치게 됐죠!

lines.en: Wow. What do you enjoy most about it?
lines.ko: 와. 그 일에서 뭐가 가장 좋아요?

lines.en: {{What I enjoy most about my job is}} the moment a student speaks with confidence. It’s challenging but rewarding. And you?
lines.ko: 제 일에서 가장 좋은 건 학생이 자신 있게 말하는 순간이에요. 힘들지만 보람 있어요. 지우 씨는요?

lines.en: I got into this field by accident. In college, I made a poster for a friend’s café, and people loved it.
lines.ko: 저는 우연히 이 분야에 들어왔어요. 대학 때 친구 카페 포스터를 만들어 줬는데, 사람들이 정말 좋아했거든요.

lines.en: So, you mean one poster changed your path?
lines.ko: 그러니까 포스터 한 장이 진로를 바꿨다는 거예요?

lines.en: Pretty much! I started out making websites for small shops. Now I’m a UX designer. It’s been quite a journey.
lines.ko: 거의 그렇죠! 처음엔 작은 가게들 웹사이트를 만들었어요. 지금은 UX 디자이너고요. 꽤 긴 여정이었어요.

lines.en: So where do you see yourself going next?
lines.ko: 그럼 앞으로는 어떤 길로 가고 싶어요?

lines.en: {{I’m hoping to move into}} UX research. And I’d like to take on more responsibility.
lines.ko: UX 리서치 쪽으로 옮기고 싶어요. 그리고 책임을 더 많이 맡고 싶어요.

lines.en: You’ve come a long way, Jiwoo. I’m sure you’ll get there.
lines.ko: 정말 많이 성장했네요, 지우 씨. 분명 해낼 거예요.

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "Career Paths · 2월 마지막 주말, 그레이스네 집에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Jiwoo: "Grace, can I ask you something? Did you always want to be a teacher?" (그레이스, 뭐 하나 물어봐도 돼요? 원래부터 선생님이 되고 싶었어요?)
2. Grace: "Not at all! I started out as a consultant in the travel industry." (전혀요! 처음엔 여행 업계에서 컨설턴트로 일했어요.)
3. Jiwoo: "Really? So how did you get into teaching?" (정말요? 그럼 어떻게 가르치는 일을 하게 됐어요?)
4. Grace: "I resigned and came to Seoul for one year, just for fun. I taught a few classes, and I ended up staying and teaching English!" (일을 그만두고 재미 삼아 1년만 서울에 왔어요. 몇 번 가르치다가 결국 눌러앉아 영어를 가르치게 됐죠!)
5. Jiwoo: "Wow. What do you enjoy most about it?" (와. 그 일에서 뭐가 가장 좋아요?)
6. Grace: "What I enjoy most about my job is the moment a student speaks with confidence. It’s challenging but rewarding. And you?" (제 일에서 가장 좋은 건 학생이 자신 있게 말하는 순간이에요. 힘들지만 보람 있어요. 지우 씨는요?)
7. Jiwoo: "I got into this field by accident. In college, I made a poster for a friend’s café, and people loved it." (저는 우연히 이 분야에 들어왔어요. 대학 때 친구 카페 포스터를 만들어 줬는데, 사람들이 정말 좋아했거든요.)
8. Grace: "So, you mean one poster changed your path?" (그러니까 포스터 한 장이 진로를 바꿨다는 거예요?)
9. Jiwoo: "Pretty much! I started out making websites for small shops. Now I’m a UX designer. It’s been quite a journey." (거의 그렇죠! 처음엔 작은 가게들 웹사이트를 만들었어요. 지금은 UX 디자이너고요. 꽤 긴 여정이었어요.)
10. Grace: "So where do you see yourself going next?" (그럼 앞으로는 어떤 길로 가고 싶어요?)
11. Jiwoo: "I’m hoping to move into UX research. And I’d like to take on more responsibility." (UX 리서치 쪽으로 옮기고 싶어요. 그리고 책임을 더 많이 맡고 싶어요.)
12. Grace: "You’ve come a long way, Jiwoo. I’m sure you’ll get there." (정말 많이 성장했네요, 지우 씨. 분명 해낼 거예요.)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. The learner plays Jiwoo in this lesson, so an answer in the first person (I'm new here instead of Jiwoo is new here) is right too; never correct that. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

2. Grace (you): "Not at all! I started out as a consultant in the travel industry." (전혀요! 처음엔 여행 업계에서 컨설턴트로 일했어요.)
3. Jiwoo (learner): "Really? So how did you get into teaching?" (정말요? 그럼 어떻게 가르치는 일을 하게 됐어요?)
4. Grace (you): "I resigned and came to Seoul for one year, just for fun. I taught a few classes, and I ended up staying and teaching English!" (일을 그만두고 재미 삼아 1년만 서울에 왔어요. 몇 번 가르치다가 결국 눌러앉아 영어를 가르치게 됐죠!)
5. Jiwoo (learner): "Wow. What do you enjoy most about it?" (와. 그 일에서 뭐가 가장 좋아요?)
6. Grace (you): "What I enjoy most about my job is the moment a student speaks with confidence. It’s challenging but rewarding. And you?" (제 일에서 가장 좋은 건 학생이 자신 있게 말하는 순간이에요. 힘들지만 보람 있어요. 지우 씨는요?)
7. Jiwoo (learner): "I got into this field by accident. In college, I made a poster for a friend’s café, and people loved it." (저는 우연히 이 분야에 들어왔어요. 대학 때 친구 카페 포스터를 만들어 줬는데, 사람들이 정말 좋아했거든요.)
8. Grace (you): "So, you mean one poster changed your path?" (그러니까 포스터 한 장이 진로를 바꿨다는 거예요?)
9. Jiwoo (learner): "Pretty much! I started out making websites for small shops. Now I’m a UX designer. It’s been quite a journey." (거의 그렇죠! 처음엔 작은 가게들 웹사이트를 만들었어요. 지금은 UX 디자이너고요. 꽤 긴 여정이었어요.)
10. Grace (you): "So where do you see yourself going next?" (그럼 앞으로는 어떤 길로 가고 싶어요?)
11. Jiwoo (learner): "I’m hoping to move into UX research. And I’d like to take on more responsibility." (UX 리서치 쪽으로 옮기고 싶어요. 그리고 책임을 더 많이 맡고 싶어요.)
12. Grace (you): "You’ve come a long way, Jiwoo. I’m sure you’ll get there." (정말 많이 성장했네요, 지우 씨. 분명 해낼 거예요.)
First say in one short sentence that they will be Jiwoo and you will read Grace. The learner speaks first: call highlight_line with 1 and invite them to start. Then go in order, one line at a time: call highlight_line with the line number before each line, read your line, and for the learner's line just wait for them to say it. If they say most of it or a good part of a long line, accept it warmly and go on; only if what they say is clearly not their line, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, give one short warm comment on how they did, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick true/false check about the scene.

Go by the answers above, not by what the learner says: if their answer is the other one, say so kindly and show the line. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/아니에요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. Give the verdict in the language you are using with this learner. Only when you are speaking Korean to them, say it as 정답은 True예요 / 정답은 False예요. What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

frame: I started out as ___. / I ended up ___ing.
head: 시작
결국 (ended up)
다음 단계
rows: I started out as a cook.
I ended up running a café.
I’m hoping to move into catering.

I’m hoping to move into management.

steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: I started out as ___. / I ended up ___ing. / I’m hoping to move into ___. Table (시작 → 결국 (ended up)):
- I started out as a cook. → I ended up running a café.
- I started out in sales. → I ended up working in marketing.
- I started out as an intern. → I ended up staying for ten years.
- I started out as a web designer. → I ended up working in UX.
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items: end up + -ing · end up in + 장소

I *ended up teaching* English. (계획에 없던 일) 
We *ended up staying* home. · I *ended up in* Seoul.

*What I enjoy most* about my job *is* the people. 
*What I enjoy most is* solving problems. (+ -ing)
errors: I ended up to teach English.
I’m hoping to move in UX research.
I’m hoping to move into UX research.
I started out like a cook.
I started out as a cook.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- end up + -ing · end up in + 장소: I ended up teaching English. (계획에 없던 일) / We ended up staying home. · I ended up in Seoul.
- What I enjoy most … is ~: What I enjoy most about my job is the people. / What I enjoy most is solving problems. (+ -ing)
Common mistakes on screen:
- I ended up to teach English. → I ended up teaching English. (end up 뒤에는 -ing.)
- I’m hoping to move in UX research. → I’m hoping to move into UX research. (새 분야로 옮길 때는 into.)
- I started out like a cook. → I started out as a cook. (직업을 말할 때는 as(~로서).)
There are 2 grammar points and 3 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: end up + -ing · end up in + 장소: I ended up teaching English. (계획에 없던 일) We ended up staying home. · I ended up in Seoul.
What I enjoy most … is ~: What I enjoy most about my job is the people. What I enjoy most is solving problems. (+ -ing)
mistakes: I ended up to teach English. → I ended up teaching English.
I’m hoping to move in UX research. → I’m hoping to move into UX research.
I started out like a cook. → I started out as a cook.

steps.note: 예) a cook / running a café → I started out as a cook, but I ended up running a café.
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) a cook / running a café → I started out as a cook, but I ended up running a café. The items (the words the learner gets for each one): a cook / running a café | an intern / staying for years | a nurse / teaching nursing | a writer / making videos.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

cards: What I enjoy most about my job is ___.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "I ended up teaching English." (내 경력); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "What I enjoy most about my job is ___." / "I ended up ___ing." / "I’m hoping to move into ___.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: I got into this field by accident.
I’ve learned a lot along the way.
I’d like to take on more responsibility.
Where do you see yourself going?
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 지금까지 걸어온 길: "I started out as ___." (처음엔 ~로 시작했어요., 보통); "I got into this field by accident." (우연히 이 분야에 들어왔어요., 보통); "I’ve learned a lot along the way." (그 과정에서 많이 배웠어요., 보통); "It’s been quite a journey." (꽤 긴 여정이었어요., 친근)
- 일에 대한 느낌: "It’s challenging but rewarding." (힘들지만 보람 있어요., 보통)
- 앞을 내다보며: "I’m looking for new challenges." (새로운 도전을 찾고 있어요., 보통); "I’d like to take on more responsibility." (더 많은 책임을 맡고 싶습니다., 정중); "I’m thinking of changing careers." (직업을 바꿀까 생각 중이에요., 보통); "Where do you see yourself going?" (앞으로 어떤 길로 가고 싶어요?, 보통)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

A: How did you get into teaching?   B: I started out ___ a consultant, but I ended up ___ English. 
A: What do you enjoy most?   B: What I enjoy most about my job ___ my students. I’m hoping to move ___ teacher training. 
낱말 상자: as · teaching · is · into
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 이야기 속 낱말 (참고): a spin-off program 파생 프로그램 · an ally 내 편, 지지자 / retain your skills 실력을 유지하다 · resistance to change 변화에 대한 거부감 / the formation of a new group 새 모임 결성 · intellectual 지적인, 학문적인
- 부드러운 말: Oh dear! 아이고(부드러운 ‘oh no’) · all too stressful 너무나 힘든 / I’m hoping to … ~하고 싶어요(I’m going to …보다 부드러운 바람)
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: How did you get into teaching? B: I started out ___ a consultant, but I ended up ___ English. / A: What do you enjoy most? B: What I enjoy most about my job ___ my students. I’m hoping to move ___ teacher training. / 낱말 상자: as · teaching · is · into
Go through every point in each tip box (for example every greeting with its time of day), one or two short sentences each, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, one blank per turn: stop at the blank, wait for them to fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: designer (디자이너), consultant (컨설턴트), adviser (조언자, 고문), network (인맥), compete (경쟁하다), path (길, 진로), challenge (도전, 어려운 일), promotion (승진), industry (업계, 산업), resign ((직장을) 그만두다), consult ((전문가와) 상담하다), skill (기술, 능력).
Go through about six, new ones first, one word per turn: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and wait for the learner to say it before the next word. Never give several words in one turn. After every two or three words, ask one tiny real question with the word you just did (for example: Are you a morning person?), wait for the answer and react; do this at least twice in this part. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: I want to specialize in research.
I got into design by accident.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: field (분야) — "the design field"; profession ((전문) 직업) — "Teaching is a great profession."; role (역할) — "a bigger role"; responsibility (책임, 맡은 일) — "more responsibility"; rewarding (보람 있는) — "challenging but rewarding"; specialize (전문으로 하다) — "I want to specialize in research."; career (경력, 직업 생활) — "a long career in travel"; opportunity (기회) — "a great opportunity"; develop (발전시키다, 기르다) — "develop new skills"; accident (by accident 우연히(앞에서는 ‘사고’)) — "I got into design by accident.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: Tell me about your career path.
I started out as ___, but I ended up ___ing.
What do you hope to do in the future?
What do you enjoy most about your work or studies?
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Tell me about your career path." (hint on screen: I started out as ___, but I ended up ___ing.)
- "What do you hope to do in the future?" (hint on screen: I’m hoping to move into ___.)
- "What do you enjoy most about your work or studies?" (hint on screen: What I enjoy most is ___.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.
questions: Tell me about your career path.
What do you hope to do in the future?

steps.title: A New Invitation
steps.text: Grace poured more tea. “Do you miss consulting?” Jiwoo asked. “Not really. The work was *all too* stressful,” said Grace. “I planned to *move back* home after a year, but Seoul felt like home. My first class here was a spin-off program *led by* an old friend. She’s still my best ally.” Jiwoo thought about her experience and her career *as a whole*. Just then, her phone buzzed. It was Daniel: “From March, I’m hosting a discussion group at our café. Grace too! Nothing too intellectual, I promise.” “*Oh dear*,” Jiwoo laughed. “His questions are hard!” “That’s the fun,” said Grace. “We won’t be beginners *for long*.”
steps.gloss: all too 너무나 · move back (살던 곳으로) 돌아가 살다 · spin-off 파생된 것 · led by ~가 이끄는 · as a whole 전체로 · oh dear 아이고(부드러운 ‘oh no’) · for long 오래
questions: Why doesn’t Grace miss consulting?
What is Daniel starting in March?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "A New Invitation". Text: "Grace poured more tea. “Do you miss consulting?” Jiwoo asked. “Not really. The work was all too stressful,” said Grace. “I planned to move back home after a year, but Seoul felt like home. My first class here was a spin-off program led by an old friend. She’s still my best ally.” Jiwoo thought about her experience and her career as a whole. Just then, her phone buzzed. It was Daniel: “From March, I’m hosting a discussion group at our café. Grace too! Nothing too intellectual, I promise.” “Oh dear,” Jiwoo laughed. “His questions are hard!” “That’s the fun,” said Grace. “We won’t be beginners for long.”" Words: all too 너무나 · move back (살던 곳으로) 돌아가 살다 · spin-off 파생된 것 · led by ~가 이끄는 · as a whole 전체로 · oh dear 아이고(부드러운 ‘oh no’) · for long 오래.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "Why doesn’t Grace miss consulting?" / "What is Daniel starting in March?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘What I enjoy most about my job is ___.’로 일에서 가장 좋은 점을 말할 수 있어요.
‘I ended up ___ing.’으로 일이 결국 어떻게 되었는지 말할 수 있어요.
‘I’m hoping to move into ___.’로 다음 단계를 말할 수 있어요.
steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘What I enjoy most about my job is ___.’로 일에서 가장 좋은 점을 말할 수 있어요.
- ‘I ended up ___ing.’으로 일이 결국 어떻게 되었는지 말할 수 있어요.
- ‘I’m hoping to move into ___.’로 다음 단계를 말할 수 있어요.
First ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence, and stop there to wait. React and praise specifically. Only then, in a later turn, end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to it, say that the next lesson is waiting for next time, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.
